title: Excitation Of Subradiant States In Atom Chains By Surface Plasmon Waves
authors: Nicola Piovella Giorgio Vimercati
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07651v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Subradiant states of a finite subwavelength atomic chain in free space offer a powerful resource for photon storage. Yet their preparation and control remain challenging experimentally. A standard technique is to drive the atoms by a laser and observe the florescence light of the long-lived subradiant modes of excitation after the laser is switched off. However, these modes are highly degenerate and form an almost continuous band in the subradiant manifold. Here we propose a new method of exciting a given subradiant state by coupling atoms to a surface plasmon wave propagating along the interface with a metallic film. By controlling the chain/surface distance we may load, store and release photons in the atoms, making them a promising tool for future quantum memories.

motivation: Subradiant states are promising for photon storage and quantum memories, but their high degeneracy makes selective excitation experimentally challenging.

result: The scheme enables excitation of a chosen subradiant state and controlled photon loading/storage/release, overcoming the degeneracy problem.
conclusion: Atomic chains coupled to surface plasmons offer a promising platform for future quantum memories with tunable photon storage capabilities.

title: Protecting Bosonic Codes From Ancilla-induced Errors With Continuous-variable Flags
authors: Thomas D\'ecultot, Ronan Gautier, Mazyar Mirrahimi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07139v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bosonic quantum error correction represents a route towards significant hardware overhead reduction for fault-tolerant quantum computation. However, controlling quantum harmonic oscillators that encode the quantum information comes with its own challenges. In many platforms such as superconducting circuits and trapped ions, the bosonic degree of freedom is controlled by an ancillary qubit whose decay during a qubit-oscillator gate propagates to the oscillator as a continuous error. Such errors generally lie beyond the scope of errors that the bosonic code is capable of correcting. We introduce the continuous-variable flag: an auxiliary oscillator coupled to the ancilla whose phase-space position encodes the continuous error corrupting the storage mode. After the gate, a heterodyne measurement of the flag estimates this continuous-variable error and a subsequent feedback control undoes it up to a bosonic code stabilizer. The scheme requires no new ingredients, as the flag is driven by the same dispersive coupling, displacements and rotations that implement the gates it is supposed to protect. We construct sequences protecting conditional rotations to all orders in ancilla decay with one flag, and conditional displacements to first order with one flag and to all orders with two. Simulations with realistic circuit-QED parameters predict more than three orders of magnitude fewer logical errors for the parity measurement of a four-component cat code, and a finite-energy GKP logical lifetime near its noiseless-ancilla bound. By discretizing continuous-variable errors, the flags introduced in this work are a useful tool for any hybrid oscillator-qubit processor, and open the route towards fault-tolerant simulation and computation with bosonic modes.

title: Pauli Flat Quantum States Mimicking Maximal Magic
authors: Pawe{\l} Cie\'sli\'nski
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07172v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum magic is a necessary resource for fault-tolerant quantum computing, capturing the departure of quantum states from the classically simulable stabiliser set. Motivated by its role in quantum information processing, we investigate the correlation structure of states that maximize the R\'enyi stabiliser entropies, focusing on the T-type and Hoggar states. Inspired by their distinctive properties, we explore the notion of Pauli flat states, defined as N-qubit states whose expectation values on all Pauli strings are equal in absolute value. These states reproduce the correlation structure of highly magical states, which could also be interpreted as a mixed variant of Pauli covariant N-qubit symmetric informationally complete (SIC) Weyl-Heisenberg fiducial states, while not necessarily possessing nontrivial quantum magic. We investigate their existence and possible constructions, including examples both inside and outside of the stabiliser polytope. To identify the latter, we examine a magic witness tailored to the introduced family of states. Finally, we discuss their entanglement and Bell nonlocality, providing a broader characterization of their quantum properties. For completeness, we find pure states with a relaxed condition on the Pauli expectations, which forces unequal elements to zero, and discuss their non-stabiliserness. Our results offer a new perspective on the relation between quantum magic and Pauli correlation structures. They hold relevance to geometrical approaches to quantum mechanics, entanglement and magic detection, as well as estimation tasks.

motivation: Quantum magic is a key resource for fault-tolerant quantum computing, and understanding the correlation structure of highly magical states may shed light on magic detection and resource theories.
method: The authors define Pauli flat states motivated by T-type and Hoggar states that maximize Rényi stabiliser entropies, then investigate their existence, constructions, and use a tailored magic witness to distinguish states inside and outside the stabiliser polytope.
result: They construct examples of Pauli flat states both within and outside the stabiliser polytope, identify them via a magic witness, and characterize their entanglement and Bell nonlocality, also finding pure states with relaxed Pauli conditions.
conclusion: The work offers a new perspective on the relationship between quantum magic and Pauli correlation structures, with implications for geometrical quantum mechanics, entanglement and magic detection, and estimation tasks.

authors: Sougato Bose Roopayan Ghosh
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07144v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Exponentially small spectral gaps are the central obstacle to adiabatic quantum annealing, yet whether such bottlenecks demand correspondingly complex entanglement remains unclear. title: Quantum Darwinism Through Apparatus-mediated Environmental Recording
authors: Tran P. H Don, Lan Nguyen Tran, Le Bin Ho
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07568v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum Darwinism explains classical objectivity through redundant environmental records of a system's pointer states. These results extend the description of quantum Darwinism to indirect measurements and clarify the conditions for reliable environmental records.

conclusion: KPZ superdiffusion in quantum systems is not limited to integrable models, establishing a broader universality class in chaotic quantum circuits.

title: Neural Correlation Learning For Quantum-Enhanced Sensing With Time-Independently Driven Rydberg Atom Arrays
authors: Tao Zhang, Xiaotian Nie, Linghui Chen
abstract: ArXiv:2610.06961v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum-enhanced sensing typically relies on preparing specific entangled states. However, engineering these states in scalable many-body systems remains challenging due to the difficulty of designing robust preparation protocols and accounting for realistic noise. We show that evolving a simple product state under native time-independent Hamiltonian dynamics in Rydberg atom arrays generates complex many-body correlations that can potentially enable quantum-enhanced parameter estimation reaching the Heisenberg limit (HL). The key challenge is then shifted to extracting the metrological information encoded in spatial correlations of measurement patterns. We introduce a neural correlation learning framework that combines Bayesian inference with neural networks trained on calibration data. Operating in a two-stage calibration-and-sensing protocol, we numerically demonstrate that this framework effectively extracts many-body correlations to saturate the Cram\'er--Rao bound dictated by the classical Fisher information. Consequently, it achieves quantum-enhanced sensitivity surpassing the standard quantum limit (SQL). Furthermore, the learned estimator is robust to realistic noise, and remains accurate in the absence of rare measurement patterns. Our results establish a hardware-efficient and scalable paradigm for quantum sensing in interacting many-body systems without requiring engineered entangled states.
tldr: A neural correlation learning framework extracts many-body correlations in driven Rydberg atom arrays to achieve quantum-enhanced sensing beyond the standard quantum limit without engineered entangled states.
motivation: Quantum-enhanced sensing typically requires entangled state preparation, which is challenging in scalable many-body systems due to protocol complexity and noise.
method: The authors evolve a simple product state under native time-independent Hamiltonian dynamics in Rydberg atom arrays and use a two-stage calibration-and-sensing protocol combining Bayesian inference with neural networks trained on calibration data.
result: The framework saturates the Cramér-Rao bound dictated by classical Fisher information, surpasses the standard quantum limit, and remains robust to realistic noise and missing rare measurement patterns.
conclusion: This establishes a hardware-efficient and scalable paradigm for quantum sensing in interacting many-body systems without requiring engineered entangled states.

title: Redundancy And Synergy In Multivariate Gaussians Via The Blackwell Order
authors: Artemy Kolchinsky
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07360v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The goal of the partial information decomposition (PID) is to quantify the redundant and synergistic information that multiple sources provide about a target. PID has many applications in machine learning, neuroscience, and other fields, but defining and computing it for high-dimensional continuous systems remains challenging. Here, we define a PID for multivariate Gaussian systems based on the Blackwell order, which formalizes when one channel is more informative than another. We prove that Gaussian channels are optimal for extracting both redundant and union information, yielding an intuitive geometric interpretation and an efficient numerical algorithm for the PID. Our union information and synergy coincide with the well-known BROJA measures, and we derive closed-form expressions for both in the case of two sources. We also argue that Blackwell redundancy (which differs from BROJA) is the only existing redundancy measure that satisfies a set of natural desiderata. We demonstrate the scalability of our method on systems with up to a thousand dimensions or sources. Our approach is illustrated on an optimal control problem, where it identifies redundant and synergistic interactions between sensor and memory.
tldr: A new partial information decomposition for multivariate Gaussian systems based on the Blackwell order, with closed-form measures and a scalable numerical algorithm.
motivation: Partial information decomposition (PID) is crucial for quantifying redundancy and synergy in complex systems, but defining and computing it for high-dimensional continuous variables remains challenging.
method: The paper defines a PID for multivariate Gaussian systems using the Blackwell order, proves that Gaussian channels are optimal for extracting redundant and union information, derives closed-form expressions for two sources, and develops an efficient numerical algorithm.
result: Union information and synergy coincide with the BROJA measures, Blackwell redundancy satisfies natural desiderata, and the method scales to systems with up to a thousand dimensions or sources.
conclusion: The work provides a principled and scalable approach to PID for Gaussian systems, illustrated on an optimal control problem, but its focus is classical information theory rather than quantum information.

title: Simultaneous Circuit Tests For Finite Reversible Models Of Quantum Control
authors: Josef Bruzzese
abstract: ArXiv:2610.06984v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A finite reversible model can approximate individual quantum gates while retaining freedom in its transition tables and preparation contexts. We formulate the simultaneous certification problem in which one stationary controller and one preparation law must reproduce an entire collection of circuit probabilities. For a specified frame catalogue, accuracy graph and calibration constraints, we give an exact shared-table feasibility formulation and distinguish certificates for a fixed table from certificates for the complete model class. A four-frame qubit example exhibits a strict separation between fitting two circuits individually and fitting them jointly. A larger exact benchmark uses 464 frames and a phase symmetry that removes preparation-prior dependence. We independently reconstruct its admissible graph and certify a sharp repeated-circuit horizon: one controller stays within probability error 1/3 through 192 blocks, whereas every allowed controller violates that threshold by block 193. A separate controller reproduces all 8,190 nonempty Hadamard-phase words of length at most twelve within the same tolerance. We also derive a finite-window spectral obstruction and finite-shot confidence tests, illustrated by a reproducible sampling experiment. The conclusions concern the stated finite reversible model classes; they do not establish a universal memory bound or a discrepancy for physical quantum hardware.
tldr: The paper formulates simultaneous certification for finite reversible models of quantum control, establishing exact shared-table feasibility, model-class certificates, and sharp repeated-circuit horizons.
motivation: Finite reversible models approximate individual quantum gates while retaining flexible transition tables and preparation contexts, motivating the need to certify one stationary controller and preparation law across an entire collection of circuit probabilities.
method: An exact shared-table feasibility formulation distinguishes certificates for a fixed table from certificates for the complete model class, supported by a 464-frame benchmark with phase symmetry, an independently reconstructed admissible graph, a finite-window spectral obstruction, and finite-shot confidence tests.
result: A four-frame qubit example shows a strict separation between fitting two circuits individually and jointly; in the larger benchmark a controller stays within error 1/3 through 192 blocks while every allowed controller violates that threshold by block 193, and another controller reproduces all 8,190 nonempty Hadamard-phase words of length at most twelve.
conclusion: The conclusions apply only to the stated finite reversible model classes and do not establish a universal memory bound or a discrepancy for physical quantum hardware.

title: Microfabrication Of Paul Wheel Trap Chip In Fused Silica By Selective Laser Etching
authors: Jakub Vejrosta, Luk\'a\v{s} \v{s}ilhan, Mojm\'ir \v{s}er\'y, Tom\'a\v{s} Fo\v{r}t, Oto Brzobohat\'y, Pavel Zem\'anek
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07813v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a rapid, mask-free fabrication workflow for the Paul wheel trap chip based on selective laser etching (SLE) of fused silica. The complete process - femtosecond laser writing, wet-chemical etching in KOH ([MATH]230 [MATH]m/h, releasing the trap geometry from a 500 [MATH]m wafer in approximately 2 h), RF magnetron sputtering of silver electrodes, and direct femtosecond laser ablation for electrode patterning - is carried out in-house, bypassing photolithographic processing and custom shadow masks entirely. Nine chips per 4-inch wafer can be produced in a single working day, reducing the fabrication lead time by more than one order of magnitude relative to the outsourced CVD diamond design. The functionality of the fabricated wheel trap chip is confirmed by a proof-of-concept microparticle trapping demonstration, in which a single microparticle was confined continuously for 72 h at atmospheric pressure. This establishes SLE of fused silica as a rapid, economically accessible fabrication platform for Paul traps in levitated-optomechanics applications.
tldr: A mask-free selective laser etching workflow is developed for fabricating Paul wheel trap chips in fused silica, demonstrated by trapping a microparticle for 72 h.
motivation: To reduce fabrication lead time and cost for Paul trap chips used in levitated optomechanics, bypassing photolithographic processing and custom shadow masks.
method: The process combines femtosecond laser writing, KOH wet etching, RF magnetron sputtering of silver electrodes, and direct femtosecond laser ablation for electrode patterning, yielding nine chips per 4-inch wafer in a single day.
result: The fabricated chip's functionality is confirmed by continuously confining a single microparticle for 72 h at atmospheric pressure, with lead time reduced by more than an order of magnitude relative to an outsourced CVD diamond design.
conclusion: Selective laser etching of fused silica is established as a rapid, economically accessible fabrication platform for Paul traps in levitated-optomechanics applications.

title: Learning Disentangled Representations With Quantum Variational Autoencoders
authors: Gaoyuan Wang, Jerry Tan, Mark Gerstein
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07196v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Variational autoencoders are powerful representation learning models that map complex data into low-dimensional latent spaces, enabling the discovery of interpretable and disentangled factors. Such representations can facilitate the interpretation and controllable generation of data describing complex scientific systems. Understanding how these factors are organized and encoded in latent space is therefore important for developing reliable representation learning models. Recently, quantum variational autoencoders (QVAEs) have been proposed as quantum representation models, demonstrating informative latent representations and improved latent-space occupancy through quantum regularization. However, it remains unclear whether and how QVAEs can learn disentangled and interpretable latent factors. A key challenge in investigating quantum latent factors is that a small number of qubits spans an exponentially large Hilbert space, making the notion of an individual quantum latent dimension nontrivial. Here, we investigate what constitutes an individual quantum latent dimension and whether it can encode a distinct factor. We develop theoretical insights into quantum latent dimensions and support them with empirical studies on representative synthetic problems, including MNIST variants. Across three datasets, we demonstrate that QVAEs can discover factorized and semantically interpretable latent representations, with individual qubits functioning as meaningful latent factors. These results establish a foundation for understanding quantum latent spaces and their potential for structured and interpretable representation learning.
tldr: This paper investigates whether quantum variational autoencoders (QVAEs) can learn disentangled and interpretable latent representations, with individual qubits acting as meaningful latent factors.
motivation: Variational autoencoders are powerful for learning interpretable representations, and QVAEs have recently emerged as quantum representation models, but it remains unclear whether and how they can learn disentangled factors given the exponentially large Hilbert space spanned by few qubits.
method: The authors develop theoretical insights into what constitutes an individual quantum latent dimension and support them with empirical studies on synthetic problems and MNIST variants across three datasets.
result: They demonstrate that QVAEs can discover factorized and semantically interpretable latent representations, with individual qubits functioning as distinct meaningful latent factors.
conclusion: These results lay a foundation for understanding quantum latent spaces and their potential for structured and interpretable representation learning.

title: Resource-Aware Grover Search For Minimum Vertex Cover
authors: Beilei Jiang, Harry Fu, Pavan Krishna Yarlagadda, Alexander Shan, Yunhe Feng, Song Fu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07252v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Minimum Vertex Cover (MVC) problem is a fundamental NP-hard combinatorial optimization problem with applications in network analysis and resource allocation. Grover's algorithm provides a quadratic reduction in query complexity for unstructured search, but existing Grover-based MVC formulations can incur substantial quantum resource overhead due to costly vertex-counting circuits and complex oracle constructions. We develop and evaluate several encoding and oracle-design strategies for reducing the qubit count, circuit depth, and gate complexity of Grover-based MVC search. First, we construct a Dicke-Parallel formulation that restricts the search to fixed-cardinality subsets, eliminating explicit vertex counting, together with a parallel edge-verification oracle that reduces feasibility-checking overhead. We then develop an Edge-Counting formulation that replaces per-edge auxiliary storage with a logarithmic-size counting register, substantially reducing ancillary-qubit requirements. Finally, we propose an Edge-Centric encoding that represents endpoint selections directly and derives vertex-selection states through incident-edge Boolean operations, enabling more depth-efficient oracle construction. Our resource analysis reveals complementary trade-offs among qubit width, circuit depth, gate count, and Grover iteration count. Edge-Counting is particularly attractive under tight qubit constraints, while Edge-Centric can reduce both circuit depth and Grover iteration count when the graph has a moderate edge count and sufficient representation multiplicity. Dicke-Parallel provides a more robust choice when such multiplicity is limited or graph density makes the edge-based search space large. These results provide practical guidance for selecting Grover-based MVC formulations according to hardware constraints and graph structure.
tldr: The paper develops and compares several encoding and oracle-design strategies for Grover-based Minimum Vertex Cover search to reduce qubit count, circuit depth, and gate complexity.
motivation: Grover-based formulations of the NP-hard Minimum Vertex Cover problem suffer large quantum resource overhead from costly vertex-counting circuits and complex oracles, limiting practical near-term implementation.
method: Three formulations are proposed: a Dicke-Parallel encoding restricting search to fixed-cardinality subsets with parallel edge verification, an Edge-Counting formulation using a logarithmic counting register, and an Edge-Centric encoding deriving vertex selections via incident-edge Boolean operations.
result: Resource analysis reveals complementary trade-offs among qubit width, circuit depth, gate count, and Grover iterations; Edge-Counting suits tight qubit budgets, while Edge-Centric reduces depth and iterations for moderate edge counts and sufficient multiplicity.
conclusion: The work provides practical guidance for selecting Grover-based MVC encodings based on hardware constraints and graph structure, though it remains an applied algorithmic-resource study rather than an information-theoretic contribution.

title: Order-Optimal Coded Caching With File And Demand Privacy
authors: Han Fang, Nan Liu, Wei Kang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.06998v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study coded caching with joint file and demand privacy: each user recovers its requested file while learning nothing about the remaining files and the other users' requests jointly. Let [MATH] and [MATH] be the numbers of files and users, and let [MATH] and [MATH] denote the cache memory and delivery rate, both normalized by the file size. For every [MATH] and every feasible cache size, we give a scheme whose worst-case delivery rate is at most [MATH] times the optimum. To reduce the memory used for file shares, the scheme secret-shares [MATH] differences relative to a reference file. Cached masks supply the correction needed to recover the requested file from its difference. For each integer [MATH], the scheme achieves [MATH] and [MATH]. To lower-bound the delivery rate, we compare the joint cache entropy of user groups under alternative demand vectors, using one fixed user's privacy constraint. Two choices of groups determine the optimal delivery rate up to constants at the scale [MATH] for [MATH]. At [MATH], the exact optimum is [MATH]. A complementary bound on joint broadcast entropy gives the minimum memory for unit delivery rate, [MATH], and the exact tradeoff on an interval ending at that memory. All schemes and bounds apply to repeated as well as distinct requests.
tldr: The paper presents order-optimal coded caching schemes and information-theoretic bounds that jointly protect file and demand privacy for all users.
motivation: Coded caching improves network efficiency but can leak information about users' requests and files, so joint privacy guarantees are needed without sacrificing order-optimal performance.
method: The scheme secret-shares differences relative to a reference file and uses cached masks for correction, while lower bounds are derived by comparing joint cache entropies of user groups under alternative demand vectors.
result: For every feasible cache size, the scheme achieves a delivery rate within a constant factor of the optimum, with exact optimal rates identified at a specific memory point and an exact memory-rate tradeoff on an interval.
conclusion: The work establishes order-optimal coded caching with strong joint file and demand privacy, providing both achievable schemes and matching bounds that apply to repeated and distinct requests.

title: Efficient And Implementation-Hardened Rblwe On Commodity Cortex-M Microcontrollers
authors: Muhammad Asim Javaid, Muhammad Adeel Pasha, Muhammad Ali Siddiqi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07820v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Efficient post-quantum cryptography on resource-constrained Internet-of-Things (IoT) devices requires implementations that exploit the target processor architecture while resisting practical implementation attacks. This paper presents an ISA-accelerated and implementation-hardened realization of Ring Binary Learning with Errors (RBLWE) encryption on a commodity ARM Cortex-M33 microcontroller. Packing four 8-bit polynomial coefficients into the byte lanes of a 32-bit register and processing them with SIMD-style instructions, together with a packed message codec, accelerates encryption and decryption, while a buffered hardware-TRNG entropy source drawn from the on-die Secure Element drives the key-generation gain. Together these give same-core cold-start speedups of [MATH], [MATH], and [MATH] for key generation, encryption, and decryption over a scalar baseline, and [MATH]/[MATH] lower encryption/decryption cycle counts than a reference Cortex-M0 implementation. On top of this accelerated core, we add four staged countermeasures: constant-time execution, fault hardening against zeroing, random-corruption, and instruction-skip faults, a Fujisaki-Okamoto (FO)-style CCA2 transform, and first-order shared (masked) CPA decryption, reporting each layer's cost individually. Binary-level inspection confirms these countermeasures survive compilation and identifies a compiler-induced masking flaw resolved with a hand-written assembly replacement. Dudect-style timing tests, debugger-assisted fault-injection campaigns, and component-level TVLA then provide implementation-level evidence for the staged protections. The results demonstrate a practical acceleration-security tradeoff for RBLWE on off-the-shelf microcontrollers and reusable architecture-aware techniques for lightweight post-quantum implementations.
tldr: Presents an ISA-accelerated and implementation-hardened RBLWE encryption for ARM Cortex-M33 microcontrollers, with staged side-channel and fault countermeasures.
motivation: Efficient post-quantum cryptography on resource-constrained IoT devices requires implementations that exploit the target architecture while resisting practical implementation attacks.
method: The work packs four 8-bit polynomial coefficients into 32-bit registers for SIMD-style processing, adds a packed message codec and hardware-TRNG entropy source, and applies constant-time execution, fault hardening, an FO-style CCA2 transform, and first-order masked CPA decryption.
result: The accelerated core achieves cold-start speedups and lower encryption/decryption cycle counts than a Cortex-M0 baseline; countermeasures are validated through Dudect-style timing tests, fault-injection campaigns, and TVLA, including a compiler-induced masking flaw fixed via hand-written assembly.
conclusion: The paper demonstrates a practical acceleration-security tradeoff for RBLWE on commodity microcontrollers and offers reusable architecture-aware techniques for lightweight post-quantum implementations.

title: Optimal Codes For The Coverage Depth Problem And The Performance Of Random Codes
authors: Roee Gross, Yitzchak Grunbaum, Matteo Bertuzzo, Eitan Yaakobi, Alberto Ravagnani
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07370v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: DNA storage systems retrieve information by randomly sampling synthesized DNA strands, making the number of reads required for successful recovery a fundamental performance measure. This motivates the coverage depth problem: for given code parameters, determine a linear code that minimizes the expected number of randomly sampled columns required to span the entire information space. While MDS codes are known to be optimal whenever they exist, identifying optimal codes in parameter regimes where MDS codes do not exist remains largely open. In this work, we derive a general formula for the expectation in the coverage depth setting, and apply this result to establish the optimality of the [MATH]-ary simplex code for the parameters that allow its existence. Moreover, we show the optimality of the [MATH]-ary Hamming code by relating coverage depth to independent sets in the dual code and exploiting log-concavity properties of matroid basis-generating polynomials. We further analyze random linear codes, derive an exact expression for their expected coverage depth, and show that, in the constant-rate regime, their additive gap from the MDS benchmark remains bounded independently of the code length.
tldr: The paper determines optimal linear codes for the coverage depth problem arising in DNA storage and analyzes the expected coverage depth of random linear codes.
motivation: DNA storage retrieves data by randomly sampling synthesized strands, so the number of reads needed to recover information is a key performance metric; minimizing this motivates the coverage depth problem where MDS codes are known to be optimal only when they exist.
method: The authors derive a general formula for the expected number of sampled columns needed to span the information space, apply it to prove optimality of q-ary simplex codes, and establish Hamming code optimality by linking coverage depth to independent sets in the dual code and using log-concavity of matroid basis-generating polynomials.
result: Simplex codes are proven optimal in the parameter regimes where they exist, Hamming codes are shown optimal via the matroid/log-concavity argument, and an exact expression for the expected coverage depth of random linear codes is obtained, revealing that at constant rate the additive gap from the MDS benchmark stays bounded regardless of code length.
conclusion: The work resolves several open cases of the coverage depth problem and quantifies how close random linear codes come to optimal MDS performance, with implications for read-count efficiency in DNA storage systems.

title: Plug-and-Play Quantum-Resistant Ble Pairing For Medical Implants Via Nfc Out-of-Band
authors: Muhammad Asim Javaid, Muhammad Shafay Tanveer Hassan, Faaiz Umer, Sotirios Panagiotou, Christos Strydis, Naveed Anwar Bhatti, Muhammad Adeel Pasha, Muhammad Ali Siddiqi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07870v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Bluetooth Low Energy (BLE) pairing establishes the cryptographic foundation for secure device communication. However, mainstream man-in-the-middle (MITM)-resistant pairing methods, such as Numeric Comparison and Passkey Entry, require user interfaces that implantable medical devices (IMDs) inherently lack, making Near-Field Communication (NFC)-assisted Out-of-Band (OOB) pairing an attractive alternative. Existing NFC-assisted OOB schemes authenticate a classical BLE key exchange that remains vulnerable to quantum attacks, while the NFC channel itself is susceptible to eavesdropping and active injection under stronger threat models. To address these limitations, we propose a lightweight, plug-and-play NFC-based OOB pairing protocol that performs a post-quantum key encapsulation mechanism (KEM) entirely over the NFC channel, ensuring that no shared secret is transmitted over NFC while reducing long-range radio-frequency (RF) exposure during pairing. The proposed protocol requires no modifications to the BLE stack and inherently resists RF battery-depletion attacks. Evaluation on an IMD-class proof-of-concept testbed demonstrates that post-quantum OOB pairing is practical on resource-constrained devices, reducing projected battery life by less than 0.57\% for Kyber-1024 and 0.56\% for FireSABER under an operational usage model relative to the MITM-vulnerable Just Works method.
tldr: The paper proposes a lightweight NFC-based out-of-band BLE pairing protocol using post-quantum KEM to secure implantable medical devices against quantum and MITM attacks.
motivation: Existing MITM-resistant BLE pairing methods require user interfaces that implantable medical devices lack, and current NFC-assisted OOB schemes remain vulnerable to quantum attacks and NFC eavesdropping/injection.
method: The protocol performs a post-quantum key encapsulation mechanism (Kyber-1024 or FireSABER) entirely over the NFC channel, transmitting no shared secret via NFC, requiring no BLE stack modifications, and resisting RF battery-depletion attacks.
result: Evaluation on an IMD-class proof-of-concept testbed shows the post-quantum OOB pairing is practical, reducing projected battery life by less than 0.57% for Kyber-1024 and 0.56% for FireSABER compared to the MITM-vulnerable Just Works method.
conclusion: Post-quantum OOB pairing is feasible for resource-constrained implantable medical devices, though the contribution is applied cryptographic protocol engineering rather than a quantum information theory advance.

title: Quantum Machine Learning For Few-Shot Impersonation Detection In Digital Account Opening
authors: Javiera Canales, Jose Ortega, Maximiliano Araya
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07242v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Identity impersonation fraud may emerge only after digital account opening, requiring an early post-onboarding approach based on behavioral and transactional signals observed shortly after activation. Confirmed cases remain rare, creating extreme class imbalance and material operational risk for digital banks. We evaluate quantum machine learning (QML) against classical one-class methods in this setting using a real 2025 cohort of 3,419 digital account openings from Banco de Creditos e Inversiones (BCI), Chile, including 8 confirmed impersonation-fraud cases (0.23% prevalence). The data were provided through an industry-research collaboration between BCI and CoreDevX LABTAV under operational constraints. The best-performing configuration used only 2 qubits and was executed on CoreDevX's SpinQ Triangulum II, a 3-qubit nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) device, enabling hardware validation beyond classical simulation. The quantum one-class classifier based on Automatic Quantum Feature Mapping (AQFM) achieves 88% recall (7 of 8 frauds detected) and 9.21% precision, corresponding to approximately 70% fewer false positives than the best-performing classical baseline at comparable recall. When its 2025-calibrated decision threshold is applied unchanged to the independent 2026 cohort, AQFM detects 20 of 31 frauds (64.5% recall) with 8.81% precision and remains the best-performing model among those evaluated.
tldr: This paper applies quantum machine learning, specifically an automatic quantum feature mapping classifier on a 2-qubit NMR device, to few-shot impersonation detection in digital account opening.
motivation: Digital banks face rare but costly impersonation fraud after account opening, and classical one-class methods may be limited by extreme class imbalance; quantum machine learning is explored as an alternative.
method: The authors evaluate a quantum one-class classifier based on Automatic Quantum Feature Mapping (AQFM) against classical one-class baselines using a 2025 cohort of 3,419 account openings with 8 fraud cases, executing the best 2-qubit configuration on a SpinQ Triangulum II NMR device.
result: AQFM achieves 88% recall and 9.21% precision on the 2025 cohort, reducing false positives by about 70% versus the best classical baseline at comparable recall, and detects 64.5% of frauds in an independent 2026 cohort with a fixed threshold.
conclusion: The study suggests quantum machine learning, even with few qubits on current NMR hardware, can improve rare-event fraud detection in financial operations, though broader quantum advantage remains unclear.

title: Connectivity Controls Variational Accessibility In Symmetry-Preserving Quantum Circuits
authors: Sahinur Reja
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07173v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Designing expressive quantum circuits for the variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) is a central challenge in simulating interacting many-body systems. Even symmetry-preserving (SP) circuits need not access the full many-body symmetry sector. We demonstrate this explicitly for the spin-[MATH] XXZ and Hubbard models, where Hamiltonian-inspired nearest-neighbor (NN) SP circuits generate restricted dynamical Lie algebras (DLAs). While these restricted manifolds can accurately represent the ground state near the free-fermion limits, [MATH] for XXZ and [MATH] for Hubbard, interactions expose inaccessible many-body directions and severely limit VQE performance even at large circuit depth. Remarkably, a minimal modification of the generator connectivity can reconstruct the full orthogonal DLA within all relevant symmetry sectors studied in this work. For XXZ model, the addition of {\it only} one SP next-to-NN single-excitation connection triggers this dramatic reconstruction, whereas the Hubbard case requires a SP correlated double-excitation;--showing that the relevant connectivity can extend from the spatial lattice to many-body configuration space. This reconstruction enlarges the tangent space and accessibility of the energy-lowering Hamiltonian direction, leading to near-unit ground-state fidelity in VQE simulations. Our results establish a direct link between generator connectivity and variational accessibility and suggest a broader circuit-design principle: identify minimal symmetry-preserving generators that enlarge the accessible many-body space rather than increasing circuit depth alone. This perspective may have broader relevance for quantum many-body simulation at the interface of condensed-matter physics and quantum computing.
tldr: Symmetry-preserving VQE circuits with nearest-neighbor connectivity generate restricted dynamical Lie algebras, limiting ground-state accuracy unless minimal nonlocal generators are added.
motivation: Designing expressive quantum circuits for variational quantum eigensolver (VQE) is challenging because symmetry-preserving circuits may not access the full many-body symmetry sector.
method: The authors analyze the dynamical Lie algebras generated by Hamiltonian-inspired nearest-neighbor symmetry-preserving generators for the XXZ and Hubbard models, and test the effect of adding minimal single- or double-excitation connections.
result: Restricted algebras represent free-fermion limits well but fail with interactions; adding one next-to-nearest-neighbor single excitation for XXZ or a correlated double excitation for Hubbard reconstructs the full algebra and yields near-unit ground-state fidelity.
conclusion: Generator connectivity directly controls variational accessibility, suggesting that minimal symmetry-preserving nonlocal connections can enlarge the accessible many-body space more effectively than increasing circuit depth alone.

title: Quantum Dynamics Of Spin Systems Using Quantum-like Resources
authors: Debadrita Saha, Ethan Dickey, William Horvat, Sabre Kais, Gregory D. Scholes
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07308v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Recent publications have introduced the concept of quantum-like (QL) bits, along with their associated QL-states and QL-gate operations, emerging from the dynamics of complex synchronized networks. The present work builds on this framework to present a simulation of quantum dynamics in spin systems. We focus on the transverse field Ising model, a widely studied Hamiltonian for interacting spin systems. We show how circuits, built using the QL analog of quantum gates, can be used to prepare an arbitrary initial wavepacket and simulate the time evolution of the resulting state for extracting physical observables such as magnetization. Beyond the statevector dynamics, we introduce a set of metrics that characterize how QL-circuit operations transform the underlying graph connections. These metrics quantify the microscopic coupling, phase coherence, and effective inter-block coupling generated by the circuit. These graph-level quantities provide constraints and design targets for potential physical implementations, indicating where interconnection resources, phase control, and effective coupling strength must be engineered in a hardware realization. Overall, this study demonstrates how classical resources can be harnessed to simulate quantum systems and we discuss the advantages and limitations.
tldr: The paper uses quantum-like bits and gates from synchronized complex networks to classically simulate quantum spin dynamics, focusing on the transverse field Ising model.
motivation: To investigate whether classical resources and quantum-like circuit operations can simulate quantum spin systems and to identify graph-level design targets for potential physical implementations.
method: They construct QL analogues of quantum gates to prepare arbitrary wavepackets and simulate time evolution of the transverse field Ising model, extracting observables such as magnetization, while defining metrics for how QL-circuit operations transform graph connections.
result: The QL circuits reproduce spin dynamics and yield graph-level metrics quantifying microscopic coupling, phase coherence, and effective inter-block coupling, providing constraints for hardware design.
conclusion: Classical quantum-like resources can simulate quantum spin dynamics, though the advantages and limitations of the approach require further study.

title: Phase Diagram And Transition Properties Of The Blume-Capel Model: A Monte Carlo Study
authors: Tenglong Li, Zhigang Feng, Jie Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07567v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The Jx-Jy Blume-Capel model, with and without an external magnetic field, is investigated using the Monte Carlo method. Our aim is to verify the location of the tricritical point, examine the existence of reentrant behavior, and study the magnetocaloric properties of this specifically designed system. In the non-field case, the critical temperature given by the Monte Carlo simulations is lower compared to the conventional antiferromagnetic square lattice. When an external magnetic field is applied, we observed signs of a one-dimensional spontaneous symmetry-breaking phase in the mixed-states regime, which is counterintuitive with secondary specific-heat peak. We take the snapshot of this state and elucidated the underlying mechanisms using mean field theory in the field of spin-1 spinor Bose-Einstein condensate . Regarding reentrant behavior, we confirmed its occurrence as the magnetic field varies, but only when the temperature is kept constant. Temperature-dependent reentrant behavior could not be identified within this system. Finally, we examined the magnetocaloric properties and found no evidence of first-order phase transitions within the region of the considered phase-transition point. Although both inverse and direct magnetocaloric effects are present and related to the mixed state, we identified that the relevant phase transitions are all of the second order.
tldr: Monte Carlo study of the Jx-Jy Blume-Capel model exploring phase transitions, tricritical point, reentrant behavior, and magnetocaloric properties with and without an external magnetic field.
motivation: To verify the location of the tricritical point, examine the existence of reentrant behavior, and investigate magnetocaloric properties in a specifically designed Blume-Capel system.
method: Monte Carlo simulations are used to study the phase diagram, supplemented by mean-field theory in the context of spin-1 spinor Bose-Einstein condensates to interpret a mixed-state regime.
result: The critical temperature is lower than the conventional antiferromagnetic square lattice; a one-dimensional spontaneous symmetry-breaking phase with a secondary specific-heat peak is observed under an external field; reentrant behavior is confirmed only for field variations at constant temperature; all phase transitions are second order.
conclusion: The Blume-Capel model exhibits rich phase behavior including a mixed state and reentrant effects, but no evidence for first-order transitions in the considered region; magnetocaloric effects are present but associated with second-order transitions.

title: The Parliament Of Observers - Against The Observable Axiom Of Quantum Mechanics
authors: Andreas D\"oring Markus Frembs
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07254v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The 'unreasonable effectiveness of mathematics in the natural sciences' may at times give the impression that natural science, especially modern theoretical physics, is all but a formal apparatus. However, a key challenge of physics remains to align everyday notions of experience -- be it directly or mediated through instruments of arbitrary sophistication -- with their mathematical formalisation. This applies in particular to quantum theory, arguably the most successful theory of physics ever invented. One of its core assumptions postulates: [MATH] Here, we argue that already this most basic premise about the quantum formalism falls apart under careful scrutiny, at least when understood for all observables at once. In other words, we challenge the role of the noncommutative algebra of bounded operators as an adequate formalisation of the 'algebra of observables', understood as (equivalence classes of) measurement procedures that admit a coherent empirical interpretation.
tldr: Challenges the standard observable axiom of quantum mechanics, arguing that the noncommutative algebra of bounded operators is not an adequate formalization of all empirically interpretable measurement procedures.
motivation: To align everyday notions of experience with their mathematical formalization in quantum theory, particularly the assumption that observables correspond to bounded operators.
method: Conceptual and foundational analysis of the algebra of observables as equivalence classes of measurement procedures, scrutinizing the noncommutative operator algebra axiom.
result: Shows that the observable axiom falls apart when understood for all observables at once, undermining the role of bounded operators as the algebra of observables.
conclusion: Calls for a refined formalization of observables in quantum mechanics that admits a coherent empirical interpretation.

title: Direct Visualization Of Non-equilibrium Heat Extraction By A Metasurface Absorber
authors: Shu Watanabe, Robert E. Simpson, Takuo Tanaka, Wakana Kubo
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07633v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metasurface heat absorption is conventionally characterized by far-field infra-red spectroscopy under equilibrium conditions. The approach provides information on the surface emissivity but does not directly reveal heat transferred by electromagnetic absorption. To understand the resulting temperature change, however, the associated heat transfer must be considered. Here, we directly observe heat extracted by electromagnetic absorption using infrared thermography. By monitoring the cooling dynamics of a copper plate placed in contact with a metasurface-integrated thermoelectric device, we show that the copper plate cools faster than one placed on an unstructured planar surface (control). This result provides direct evidence of heat transfer from the adjacent solid to the metasurface; revealing a metasurface-mediated electromagnetic absorption heat transfer mechanism. These findings provide new insight into nonequilibrium thermal processes enabled by metasurface absorbers.
tldr: The paper directly visualizes non-equilibrium heat extraction by a metasurface absorber using infrared thermography of a copper plate coupled to a thermoelectric device.
motivation: Conventional far-field infrared spectroscopy characterizes metasurface absorption under equilibrium conditions but does not directly reveal the heat transferred by electromagnetic absorption or the resulting temperature changes.
method: The authors monitor the cooling dynamics of a copper plate placed in contact with a metasurface-integrated thermoelectric device and compare it to a control copper plate on an unstructured planar surface using infrared thermography.
result: The copper plate on the metasurface cools faster than the control, providing direct evidence of heat transfer from the adjacent solid to the metasurface and revealing a metasurface-mediated electromagnetic absorption heat-transfer mechanism.
conclusion: These findings offer new insight into nonequilibrium thermal processes enabled by metasurface absorbers, though the work is classical photonic/thermal engineering rather than quantum information or quantum thermodynamics.

title: Demonstration Of Parallel Multi-QPU Execution For Fragment-Based Quantum Chemistry Using On-Premises Hardware
authors: Nils Herrmann, Mariam Akhtar, Luke W. Bertels, Leigh Cameron, Raymond Chan, Lei Cheng, Daniel Claudino, Mark de Burgh, Simon Gemmell, Rugang Geng, Geoff Gillett, Travis Humble, Stephan Irle, John P. Mcmahon, Christian Ortiz, Florian Preis, Andreas Sawadsky, Bianca Sawyer, Reuben Singer, Sai Meghana Tunikipati, Cameron Walters, Lachlan Whichello, Adam Zegelin, Marcus W. Doherty
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07702v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Fragment molecular orbital (FMO) quantum chemistry offers a natural route to parallel quantum computing: large molecular calculations can be decomposed into smaller quantum subproblems that can, in principle, run concurrently. Their practical benefit on real quantum hardware, however, has remained unclear. We demonstrate parallel FMO calculations on three room-temperature diamond-based 'Quoll' quantum computers installed on-site at the Oak Ridge Leadership Computing Facility. Helium clusters (He[MATH], [MATH]) served as a testbed for total energy calculations using the Quantum Wave Function Sampler (QWFS), a selected configuration interaction (SCI) approach. We compare two execution modes: synchronous shot-parallel execution, in which quantum processors jointly sample QWFS circuits and combine their SPAM-corrected counts into a single probability distribution; and asynchronous fragment-parallel execution, in which processors independently evaluate FMO fragments using device-specific optimized circuits. Both modes increase quantum sampling throughput without systematic loss of accuracy. The three-QPU shot-parallel workflow reaches a parallel efficiency of [MATH], while the fragment-parallel workflow achieves a measured efficiency of [MATH], increasing to [MATH] when excluding the non-useful idle time associated with non-interruptible submitted jobs. In both cases, the assembled FMO-QWFS energies remain chemically accurate compared to the classical ideal. These results provide a proof-of-concept demonstration that parallel quantum execution can improve the practical throughput of quantum chemistry workflows on prototype hardware, motivating the development of future HPC environments with many fault-tolerant quantum processors operating as a distributed resource for molecular and materials simulation.
tldr: Demonstrates parallel quantum chemistry calculations on multiple diamond-based quantum computers, achieving improved throughput without loss of accuracy.
motivation: To assess the practical benefit of distributing quantum chemistry workloads across multiple quantum processors and enable HPC integration.
method: Used fragment molecular orbital (FMO) decomposition and Quantum Wave Function Sampler (QWFS) on three room-temperature diamond-based Quoll QPUs, comparing synchronous shot-parallel and asynchronous fragment-parallel execution modes for helium clusters.
result: Both execution modes increased sampling throughput without systematic accuracy loss, with parallel efficiencies measured and energies remaining chemically accurate compared to classical ideal.
conclusion: Proof-of-concept shows parallel quantum execution can improve throughput for quantum chemistry workloads.

title: Pulsation Of Quantum Walk On Finite Graph
authors: Etsuo Segawa Taisuke Hosaka
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07768v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study discrete-time quantum walks on weighted graphs, where every edge in an edge cut set is assigned a small weight [MATH]. The parameter [MATH] represents the strength of the connections through the cut edges: as [MATH], these connections vanish, and the graph decomposes into the connected components obtained by removing the cut edges. We refer to these weighted cut edges as {\it weak edges}. We show that, for sufficiently small [MATH] and on the time scale [MATH], the finding probabilities between the connected components are asymptotically described by a continuous-time wave equation on a reduced graph, whose vertices represent the connected components and whose edges represent the weak edges connecting them. The wave equation is governed by a symmetric weighted Laplacian determined by the reduced graph and the number of arcs contained in the components. Consequently, finding probabilities of leading-term are independent of the detailed internal structures of the components. We further show that this wave equation has the same form as Newton's equation of motion for a classical spring-mass system on the reduced graph.
tldr: The paper analyzes discrete-time quantum walks on weighted graphs with weak cut edges, showing that at long times the inter-component finding probabilities are governed by a continuous-time wave equation on a reduced graph.
motivation: Understanding how quantum walks behave on graphs with weakly connected components can reveal effective coarse-grained dynamics and connections to classical wave or mechanical systems.
method: The authors introduce small weights on cut edges, take the limit of vanishing weak connections, and derive an asymptotic continuous-time wave equation on a reduced graph using a symmetric weighted Laplacian.
result: For sufficiently small edge weights and suitable time scales, the leading-order finding probabilities depend only on the reduced graph and the number of arcs in each component, not on the internal structure of the components. The wave equation matches Newton's equations for a classical spring-mass system.
conclusion: The work establishes a rigorous link between discrete-time quantum walks with weak edges and effective continuous-time wave/mechanical dynamics, showing universal coarse-grained behavior on reduced graphs.

title: Quantum Telescopy With Realistic Anti-correlated Optical Fields As References
authors: Z. Y. Ou Xuan Tang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07806v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Quantum telescopy, proposed by Grottesman et al., uses spatially entangled single-photon states to modify HBT stellar interferometry, potentially surpassing Michelson interferometry in resolution without baseline limits. However, finite source bandwidth, non-unit efficiency, detector response times, and celestial light bandwidth all affect its effectiveness. In this work, we consider a spatially entangled singe-photon state generated by beam-splitting a practical anti-bunched photon source from resonance fluorescence, which is a common method of generating single-photon states, and evaluate the signal level in quantum telescopy with inclusion of imperfection of detection system and finite bandwidth of celestial light. Here, given the incoming light, we optimize the parameters of the anti-bunched photon source and the detector system for the best signal-to-noise ratio (SNR), which can match that of the Michelson method in the ideal case but is always smaller in the realistic case. Alternatively, weak coherent states from heavily attenuated lasers can replace the entangled single-photon state but suffer low signal level, similar to HBT method. We find that the SNR with a realistic anti-bunched source for producing the reference fields can still beat the SNR of the coherent state scheme in the weak incoming field limit. The optimized parameters for the anti-bunched source and detection system will be a guide for future experimental endeavor.
tldr: This paper analyzes quantum telescopy using realistic anti-bunched single-photon sources as references, optimizing signal-to-noise ratio under detection and bandwidth imperfections and comparing to Michelson and coherent-state schemes.
motivation: Quantum telescopy with spatially entangled photons could improve stellar interferometry, but finite source bandwidth, detector inefficiency, and celestial bandwidth degrade performance, requiring a realistic assessment.
method: The authors model a spatially entangled single-photon state from beam-splitting an anti-bunched resonance-fluorescence source and optimize source and detector parameters for maximal SNR, including detection imperfections and finite celestial light bandwidth.
result: The optimized realistic anti-bunched source can match ideal Michelson interferometry in SNR but is always worse in realistic conditions; however, in the weak incoming-field limit it still outperforms a weak coherent-state scheme, which resembles HBT.
conclusion: Practical anti-bunched photon sources are preferable to coherent states for reference fields in weak-field quantum telescopy, and the optimized parameters offer guidance for future experiments.

title: A Structure-aware Construction Of Quantum Bpx Preconditioners For Q1 Finite Element Discretizations Of Reaction-diffusion Problems
authors: Yin Yang, Yue Yu, Long Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.06987v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a structure-aware construction of quantum BPX preconditioners for Q1 finite element discretizations of constant-coefficient reaction--diffusion equations on the unit cube, including the Poisson equation. Building on existing quantum finite element and finite difference methods, we express the preconditioned operator through explicit one-dimensional maps, tensor products, and norm-preserving interlevel transfers. Symmetric preconditioning gives multilevel coefficients, and its favorable conditioning alone does not ensure efficient recovery of a state in the original finite element nodal basis. We instead use the local [MATH]-orthonormal basis underlying the construction as the output representation of the same finite element function. Its coefficient norm equals the continuous [MATH] norm. Assuming direct access to the preconditioned right-hand side, we prepare this orthonormal coefficient state with a represented function error at most [MATH]. The expected query complexity is \[ \!\Big(dL^3}{\|u\|_{L^2}} \log\!\Big(2+}{\varepsilon}\Big)\Big), \] where [MATH] is the exact solution, [MATH] is the right-hand side, [MATH] is the spatial dimension, and [MATH] for mesh width [MATH]. The bound holds for [MATH] and depends only polylogarithmically on mesh refinement for fixed continuous data. We also analyze linear-functional estimation and illustrate the construction and continuous error bounds with a one-dimensional UnitaryLab experiment.
tldr: The paper constructs structure-aware quantum BPX preconditioners for Q1 finite element discretizations of reaction-diffusion and Poisson problems on the unit cube, preparing an M-orthonormal coefficient state with bounded represented-function error.
motivation: Solving PDEs such as reaction-diffusion and Poisson equations efficiently is important, and quantum computing offers potential speedups; existing quantum finite element/finite difference methods motivate building well-conditioned quantum preconditioners.
method: The preconditioned operator is expressed via explicit one-dimensional maps, tensor products, and norm-preserving interlevel transfers; the output state is prepared in the local M-orthonormal basis underlying the symmetric multilevel preconditioner, with complexity analysis for state preparation and linear-functional estimation, plus a 1D UnitaryLab experiment.
result: Assuming direct access to the preconditioned right-hand side, the orthonormal coefficient state achieves represented-function error at most epsilon with expected query complexity scaling as (d L^3 / ||u||_{L2}) log(2 + 1/epsilon), depending only polylogarithmically on mesh refinement for fixed continuous data.
conclusion: The structure-aware quantum BPX preconditioner yields favorable conditioning and provable continuous error bounds, enabling efficient quantum preparation of finite element solutions, with linear-functional estimation also analyzed.

title: Conformal Invariance Of The Six-vertex Model's Height Function
authors: Emile Averous, Hugo Duminil-Copin, Tiancheng He, Piet Lammers, Ioan Manolescu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07454v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we show that the height function of the six-vertex model in simply connected domains with piecewise constant boundary conditions converges to the Gaussian Free Field (GFF) with Dirichlet boundary conditions. This implies the conformal invariance of the scaling limit of the model. The argument relies on the full plane GFF convergence combined with Reflexion Positivity and qualitative estimates. The proof works for a wide range of spectral parameters [MATH] (among which [MATH] close to [MATH], and between [MATH] and [MATH]) making this paper the first instance of a conformal invariance result for a continuum of models. The paper has consequences for other models, including the FK percolation with cluster-weight [MATH] and the Ashkin-Teller model, which we will pursue in future work.
tldr: The paper proves that the height function of the six-vertex model in simply connected domains with piecewise constant boundary conditions converges to the Gaussian Free Field with Dirichlet boundary conditions, establishing conformal invariance for a continuum of models.
motivation: Conformal invariance of scaling limits is a central theme in statistical mechanics, and the six-vertex model is a paradigmatic integrable model where such a result was previously known only for isolated parameters.
method: The proof combines full-plane Gaussian Free Field convergence with reflection positivity and qualitative estimates to extend the convergence to simply connected domains with boundary conditions.
result: The height function converges to the Gaussian Free Field with Dirichlet boundary conditions for a wide range of spectral parameters, yielding the first conformal invariance result for a continuum of models, with consequences for FK percolation and the Ashkin-Teller model.
conclusion: This work establishes conformal invariance of the six-vertex model's scaling limit across a continuum of parameters, opening the door to similar results for related statistical mechanics models.

title: Spontaneous Symmetry Breaking At Any Temperature In A Local One-dimensional Model
authors: Andrew Lucas
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07693v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We present a one-dimensional classical statistical physics model on an infinite lattice with nearest-neighbor interactions and local state space [MATH], with a ``helical" symmetry group [MATH] mixing flavor symmetry with spatial translation. For any [MATH], we construct an uncountable infinity of DLR (Gibbs) states parameterized by [MATH], with a free [MATH] flavor symmetry group action; as such, we interpret the model as exhibiting spontaneous symmetry breaking at any temperature. The most general DLR state we construct is interpreted as an infinite sequence of localized domain walls separating a pair of asymptotic ``symmetry sectors". Although any normalizable Gibbs state necessarily breaks a countably infinite freely-acting symmetry group, a natural regularization of the problem to (arbitrarily) large but finite systems with periodic boundary conditions has measure concentration in disjoint and far-separated symmetry-related clusters in the (now unique) Gibbs state, which justifies our interpretation of spontaneous symmetry breaking on the infinite line. A modification of the model with local state space [MATH] must break a continuous helical symmetry at any temperature. This is not a contradiction with the Mermin-Wagner Theorem, because this continuous helical symmetry is non-compact and does not commute with translation.
tldr: The paper constructs a one-dimensional classical statistical physics model with a helical symmetry that exhibits spontaneous symmetry breaking at any temperature, using DLR states and domain wall interpretations.
motivation: To demonstrate that spontaneous symmetry breaking can occur at any temperature in a local one-dimensional model, circumventing the Mermin-Wagner theorem through a non-compact symmetry that does not commute with translation.
method: The author constructs uncountable DLR (Gibbs) states parameterized by symmetry sectors, interprets them as infinite sequences of localized domain walls, and analyzes a finite-size regularization with periodic boundary conditions to justify the interpretation.
result: For any temperature, an uncountable infinity of DLR states with a free flavor symmetry group action is constructed, and a modified model with a continuous helical symmetry is shown to break that symmetry at any temperature.
conclusion: The results show that the Mermin-Wagner theorem does not forbid symmetry breaking in one dimension when the symmetry is non-compact and does not commute with spatial translation, providing a classical statistical mechanics counterexample.

title: Convergence Without Finite Exactness In The Eigenstate Quantum Bootstrap
authors: Daniel Keren Ye Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07775v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The eigenstate quantum-mechanical bootstrap can converge to the physical moment set while remaining nonexact at every finite order. We prove this for a one-dimensional quasi-exactly solvable sextic oscillator at explicitly known eigenvalues, including excited levels. At every finite order, the lower and upper bounds on [MATH] remain strictly below and above its physical value, even after adjoining arbitrary finite polynomial Gram tests and all eigenstate-annihilator relations visible in the retained moment space. Hence neither side of the centered observable admits a finite sum-of-squares certificate modulo the eigenstate annihilator. The gap persists under any finite set of additional localizing constraints whose weights are strictly positive on polynomial vectors. We then prove convergence for polynomial Schr\"odinger operators satisfying explicit sum-of-squares confinement and derivative bounds. The eigenstate relations give moment estimates uniform in the truncation order; these yield a regular Schr\"odinger representation supported on the prescribed eigenspace. Finally, a four-mode extension combines this fixed-observable obstruction with feasible position moments having no positive representing measure at every finite order. At level three, this construction yields nonphysical feasible points with strictly positive definite moment matrices.
tldr: The paper proves that the eigenstate quantum bootstrap can converge to physical moments without achieving finite-order exactness for quasi-exactly solvable and polynomial Schrödinger operators.
motivation: To understand whether finite-order moment constraints, including sum-of-squares certificates and eigenstate annihilator relations, can exactly capture physical quantum expectations or must always leave a gap.
method: The authors analyze a one-dimensional sextic oscillator with known eigenvalues and extend to polynomial Schrödinger operators under confinement and derivative bounds, using moment estimates and Gram matrix tests.
result: At every finite order, the lower and upper bounds remain strictly below and above the physical value, so no finite sum-of-squares certificate exists modulo the eigenstate annihilator; a four-mode extension yields nonphysical feasible points with positive definite moment matrices.
conclusion: The eigenstate bootstrap can converge to the correct physical moment set while never being exact at any finite truncation, highlighting fundamental limitations of finite-order certificate methods in quantum moment problems.

title: A Numerical And Efficient Model For Thermo-field Electron Emission Calculations
authors: Salvador Barranco C\'arceles, Andreas Kyritsakis, Anthony Ayari
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07013v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: As electron sources are reduced in size, fabricated in new materials, or pushed for performance, the analytical formulations for thermo-field electron emission, namely Fowler-Nordheim and Murphy-Good equations and their JWKB-based extensions, are increasingly applied out of the range of conditions for which they were derived. We present GETELEC-3, an open-source code that replaces them with a direct numerical solution of the one-dimensional time-independent Schr\"odinger equation (1D-TISE). Several methods to solve the 1D-TISE have been implemented to test for speed, robustness, and solution's uncertainty. The Noumerov algorithm is found to be quickest, with the solution uncertainty below 1%, and together with an optimised kernel that advances all electron energies in parallel, the cost of calculating the current density is reduced to a few milliseconds - comparable to the JWKB evaluation. To further boost the calculation speed, especially in complicated barriers, a neural network has been trained on the residual of the logarithm of the semiclassical reference and it reproduces the current density better than 0.4% at a fraction of the computational cost. The code is developed for metals and semiconductors, accepts arbitrary potentials and density of states, and comes with a user-friendly interface and compiled executable to democratise rigorous electron emission calculations and data analysis.
tldr: GETELEC-3 is an open-source numerical solver of the 1D time-independent Schrödinger equation for thermo-field electron emission, using the Noumerov algorithm and a neural-network surrogate to compute current densities quickly and accurately.
motivation: Analytical formulas like Fowler-Nordheim and Murphy-Good are increasingly used beyond their validity range as electron sources shrink and adopt new materials, so a rigorous yet efficient numerical alternative is needed.
method: The authors directly solve the 1D-TISE with several algorithms (Noumerov being fastest, <1% uncertainty), parallelize over electron energies with an optimized kernel, and train a neural network on the residual of the semiclassical log-current to further accelerate computation.
result: The numerical approach computes current densities in a few milliseconds, comparable to JWKB evaluation, while the neural network reproduces current densities to better than 0.4% at much lower computational cost.
conclusion: GETELEC-3 democratizes rigorous electron emission calculations for metals and semiconductors with arbitrary potentials and density of states via a user-friendly interface, but it addresses condensed-matter/electron-source modeling rather than quantum information or thermodynamics.

title: Crossover Of Magnetodipole And Electrodipole Contributions In The Broadband Magneto-optics Of Bismuth-substituted Iron Garnets
authors: Nika Gribova
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07595v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work presents a comprehensive macroscopic electrodynamic framework isolating the magnetodipole (MD) and electrodipole (ED) contributions to the magneto-optical effects in bismuth-substituted iron garnet. By rigorously incorporating the dispersive magnetic permeability tensor, the dominance of the MD mechanism in the terahertz (THz) gap is demonstrated. In the mid-infrared (MIR) to near-infrared (NIR) domain, a fundamental spectral crossover is revealed where the magnitudes of the MD and ED contributions exactly equalize, invalidating the widespread assumption that magnetic contributions vanish uniformly at infrared frequencies. Furthermore, it is shown that interfacial phase shifts uniquely dictate how these competing mechanisms project onto observable rotation and ellipticity, yielding an inverted spectral hierarchy between transmission (Faraday) and reflection (polar and longitudinal Kerr) geometries. Most notably, the transverse Kerr effect for s-polarized light is established to be exclusively driven by the off-diagonal magnetic permeability. While strictly zero under the conventional ED approximation, the s-polarized transverse Kerr effect emerges as a robust, free of the gyroelectric contribution probe of MD activity in the THz and MIR--NIR regimes, yielding a THz response two orders of magnitude larger than its p-polarized counterpart.
tldr: A macroscopic electrodynamic study of magnetodipole and electrodipole contributions to magneto-optical effects in bismuth-substituted iron garnets, revealing a spectral crossover and a THz-enhanced transverse Kerr effect.
motivation: The widespread assumption that magnetic contributions vanish uniformly at infrared frequencies is challenged, motivating a clear separation of magnetodipole and electrodipole mechanisms in magneto-optics.
method: The authors develop a comprehensive macroscopic electrodynamic framework that rigorously incorporates the dispersive magnetic permeability tensor and interfacial phase shifts to isolate MD and ED contributions.
result: They demonstrate MD dominance in the THz gap, a fundamental MD–ED crossover in the MIR–NIR domain, and an s-polarized transverse Kerr effect driven exclusively by off-diagonal magnetic permeability, with a THz response two orders of magnitude larger than its p-polarized counterpart.
conclusion: The s-polarized transverse Kerr effect emerges as a robust, gyroelectric-free probe of magnetodipole activity, invalidating the conventional ED approximation and enabling sensitive magneto-optical characterization in THz and MIR–NIR regimes.

title: Comparing The Reliability Of Coherent Systems With Heterogeneous, Dependent And Distribution-free Components
authors: Nuria Torrado
abstract: ArXiv:2610.06869v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, there has been a growing interest in comparing the reliability of systems with dependent components. Most of the recent works consider Archimedean copulas to define the dependency structure of systems and examine specific familiy of distributions. In this work, we provide distribution-free results to compare, in the usual stochastic order under some majorization conditions, coherent systems with heterogeneous and dependent components where the dependency structure can be defined by any copula. Applications of our main results for specific copulas and different families of marginal distributions are also given.
tldr: This paper provides distribution-free stochastic-order comparisons for coherent systems with heterogeneous and dependent components using copulas and majorization.
motivation: There is growing interest in comparing reliability of systems with dependent components, but existing results often rely on specific Archimedean copulas or marginal distributions.
method: The authors derive distribution-free comparison results in the usual stochastic order under majorization conditions, allowing the dependency structure to be any copula.
result: They obtain general comparison theorems and illustrate them with specific copulas and families of marginal distributions.
conclusion: The work extends reliability comparison methods to a broader class of dependent heterogeneous coherent systems without restricting the copula family.

title: Entropy-Based Goodness-of-Fit Tests For Generalized $\kappa$ -Gaussian Distributions
authors: Konstantinos Zografos Mehmet Siddik Cadirci
abstract: ArXiv:2610.06873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce this class of multivariate Kappa-Gaussian distributions by maximizing a type of Kaniadakis [MATH] entropy subject to certain first- and second-moment constraints. This differs slightly from the approach of R\'enyi and Tsallis, because the [MATH]-entropy arises from a relativity-consistent deformation of the exponential and logarithmic functions and yields a family of distributions whose tails follow a power law, a family that actually reverts to the standard Gaussian distribution as [MATH]. We then create a [MATH]-nearest-neighbor (NN) estimator for [MATH]-entropy and describe it using the difference between two NN functionals involving sums of powers. Next, we establish [MATH]-consistency and asymptotic normality, using the well-known subadditive Euclidean functional and moment expansion framework for NN entropy estimators. Furthermore, using a scaling identity for the [MATH]-exponential, we derive a closed-form formula for the entropy of the [MATH]-Gaussian distribution itself. From this, we determine the exact threshold value [MATH] at which the distribution preserves finite variance; this is analogous to the ``degrees of freedom [MATH]'' condition in the Student's-[MATH] distribution. With these components, we construct a non-parametric goodness-of-fit test and then verify it through simulations. Finally, we mention the Sharma--Mittal entropy, which combines the R\'enyi and Tsallis entropies as a natural direction for future work.
tldr: This paper introduces multivariate kappa-Gaussian distributions by maximizing Kaniadakis entropy under moment constraints and develops nearest-neighbor entropy estimators for goodness-of-fit tests.
motivation: The authors aim to generalize Gaussian distributions using a relativistic deformation of exponential and logarithmic functions, yielding power-law tails and a new entropy-based statistical framework.
method: They maximize Kaniadakis entropy subject to first- and second-moment constraints, construct a nearest-neighbor estimator for kappa-entropy, prove consistency and asymptotic normality using Euclidean functional and moment expansion techniques, and derive closed-form entropy and a finite-variance threshold.
