result: Evaluated on real-world vulnerability evidence, POLAR improves threat ranking and mitigation retrieval across heterogeneous incidents and zero-day settings, producing evidence-linked intermediate assessments.
conclusion: Evidence synthesis provides a practical foundation for LLM-based cyber decision support, but the work is not related to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Metric-Based Equilibrium Selection In Noncooperative Differentiable Games
authors: Karan Mahesh, Runyu Zhang, Michael R. Benjamin, Gioele Zardini
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07307v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Metric conditioning can change which equilibrium attracts learning dynamics without moving the equilibria of a differentiable game. We study how to use state-dependent symmetric positive-definite (SPD) metrics to select among known equilibria by keeping a designated equilibrium attracting while making a rival unstable. Building on classical results on matrix stability under positive-definite multiplication, we characterize when such destabilization is possible and show how restricting the metric to act independently on each player limits the stability changes that can be achieved at differential Nash equilibria. We then combine a stabilizing metric at the selected equilibrium with a destabilizing metric at the rival through smooth interpolation, yielding a single metric field that preserves every equilibrium of the game while assigning the desired local stability types. We also derive a step-size condition for implementing the method in discrete time. The approach is validated on a continuous-commitment stag hunt and an entropy-regularized iterated prisoner's dilemma, where it selects the desired equilibrium in both settings.
tldr: The paper studies how state-dependent SPD metrics can selectively stabilize one equilibrium while destabilizing a rival in differentiable games.
motivation: Equilibrium selection in multi-agent learning is challenging because standard gradient dynamics may converge to undesirable equilibria. The authors aim to control which equilibrium attracts learning dynamics without changing the game's equilibria.
method: They characterize stability changes achievable by positive-definite metric multiplication, combine stabilizing and destabilizing metrics via smooth interpolation, and derive a discrete-time step-size condition.
result: The approach preserves all equilibria while assigning desired local stability types, and is validated on a continuous-commitment stag hunt and an entropy-regularized iterated prisoner's dilemma.
conclusion: Metric conditioning provides a principled way to select among known equilibria in differentiable games, with practical discrete-time implementation and empirical validation.

title: From Sandbox To Enforcement: Confidence-Qualified Threat Intelligence For Critical Infrastructure
authors: Nikolaos Kekatos, Mihaela Curc\u{a}, Georgios Koutidis, Mihai Nena, Tom Nianios, Robert-\c{s}tefan \c{s}andru, Michael Ioannou, Charalambos Bratsas
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07310v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Security operations centres and national incident-response teams defending critical infrastructure collect abundant threat data yet struggle to turn it into actionable intelligence. A malware sandbox produces detailed behavioural evidence, but as a large, unranked report whose confidence is unstated. We present CG-CTI, an operational pipeline that converts live sandbox output (CAPEv2) into STIX 2.1, correlates it in a knowledge graph with other critical-infrastructure sensors, and attaches to every intelligence object an explicit confidence status derived from provenance, cross-source corroboration, and observation durability. This status gates automated action: only corroborated intelligence is eligible for automated enforcement, while lower-confidence objects are routed to analyst review or kept as context. A grounded language-model stage then narrates the confidence-qualified evidence, where each statement either cites a supporting object or is marked unsupported, so fabricated references are removed before analyst review. We implement CG-CTI within the CYBERGUARD project, whose consortium includes Romania's national cyber-security directorate, and evaluate it against the live sandbox on a labelled malware corpus, measuring conversion validity, indicator yield, technique coverage, corroboration, enforcement eligibility, latency, and summary grounding. CG-CTI turns fragmented sandbox output into corroborated, confidence-ranked, and auditable intelligence for critical-infrastructure defence.
tldr: CG-CTI is an operational pipeline that converts live malware sandbox output into confidence-qualified STIX 2.1 threat intelligence for critical infrastructure defense.
motivation: Security operations centers and incident-response teams collect abundant threat data but struggle to turn it into actionable, trustworthy intelligence because sandbox reports are large, unranked, and have unstated confidence.
method: The pipeline ingests CAPEv2 sandbox output, converts it to STIX 2.1, correlates it in a knowledge graph with other critical-infrastructure sensors, assigns explicit confidence status from provenance, corroboration, and observation durability, gates automated enforcement, and uses a grounded language model to narrate evidence with citation support.
result: Evaluated against a live sandbox and a labelled malware corpus, the system measures conversion validity, indicator yield, technique coverage, corroboration, enforcement eligibility, latency, and summary grounding.
conclusion: CG-CTI turns fragmented sandbox output into corroborated, confidence-ranked, and auditable intelligence for critical-infrastructure defense.

title: NetAgent: Multi-Task Agentic Network Traffic Analysis Made Practical
authors: Hao Fu, Dawn Song, Peng Gao
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07386v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Network traffic analysis is central to network security, spanning tasks from intrusion detection to encrypted traffic classification. Existing approaches either train task-specific models that generalize poorly or rely on costly traffic foundation models that still struggle under distribution shift. We present NetAgent, the first agentic framework for multi-task traffic analysis. Through a carefully designed agent loop, NetAgent supports complex task understanding, on-the-fly decomposition and orchestration, dynamic replanning, and long-horizon analysis, without task-specific training. It introduces five key designs: (1) knowledge-augmented workflow planning that maps attack knowledge to traffic features to bridge the semantic gap; (2) a comprehensive tool action space with 150+ verified tools extracted from 50+ published systems; (3) a unified code execution space for flexible action composition; (4) a three-tier memory for long-term knowledge consolidation; and (5) sandboxing and runtime repair for reliable execution. Across 9 major benchmarks, NetAgent outperforms all baselines (23 single-task and 5 multi-task) on nearly all tasks and generalizes substantially better to unseen traffic distribution (90.04% F1 vs. 2.74% and 3.04% for the best single-task and multi-task baselines) and under realistic background shift (4.85-point F1 drop vs. 74.88-point and 74.80-point drop for the best single-task and multi-task baselines). These results reveal that existing methods owe much of their reported success to overfitting dataset-specific patterns and degrade sharply in realistic network environments, while NetAgent's agentic design remains accurate, generalizable, and robust.
tldr: NetAgent is an agentic framework for multi-task network traffic analysis that uses knowledge-augmented planning, a large tool set, code execution, memory, and sandboxing to generalize better than task-specific or foundation-model baselines.
motivation: Existing network traffic analysis methods either train task-specific models that generalize poorly or rely on costly traffic foundation models that still struggle under distribution shift.
method: The framework employs a carefully designed agent loop for task understanding, decomposition, orchestration, dynamic replanning, and long-horizon analysis without task-specific training, integrating five key designs: knowledge-augmented workflow planning, 150+ tools from 50+ systems, unified code execution, three-tier memory, and sandboxing with runtime repair.
result: Across 9 benchmarks, NetAgent outperforms 23 single-task and 5 multi-task baselines on nearly all tasks, achieving 90.04% F1 under unseen traffic distribution (vs. 2.74% and 3.04%) and only a 4.85-point F1 drop under realistic background shift (vs. ~75-point drops for baselines).
conclusion: Agentic design enables accurate, generalizable, and robust network traffic analysis, revealing that existing methods often overfit dataset-specific patterns and degrade sharply in realistic network environments.

title: Cores Characterize The One-Pass Streaming Complexity Of CSPs
authors: Joshua Brakensiek, Aaron Putterman, Amatya Sharma, Santhoshini Velusamy
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07455v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study the one-pass streaming complexity of CSPs over a fixed finite relation [MATH] under three natural objectives: [MATH], deciding whether all constraints can be satisfied; [MATH]-[MATH], approximately minimizing the number of unsatisfied constraints; and [MATH], exactly computing the maximum number of satisfied constraints. Sharma and Velusamy (ESA 2026) characterized the streaming complexity of satisfiability for CSPs with literals using the non-redundancy parameter [MATH], which roughly measures the largest instance in which every constraint is independently necessary. For the most general setting without literals, they obtained the corresponding characterization for Boolean relations and showed obstacles to extending their techniques to larger domains. Kol, Paramonov, Saxena, and Yu (ITCS 2023) similarly characterized the streaming complexity of [MATH] for Boolean CSPs with literals in terms of the degree deg[MATH] of the relation when written as a polynomial, while without literals, the corresponding result was known only for [MATH]. For all three of the objectives we study, we give tight characterizations for unweighted CSP instances over arbitrary finite domains. The streaming algorithms we provide are deterministic, while the corresponding bounds are tight up to polylogarithmic factors, even against randomized algorithms. The central idea in all three results is a reduction of [MATH] to its core, a canonical subrelation of [MATH] which admits gadgets that allow for the hard-pinning (or fixing) of variables.
tldr: The paper gives tight one-pass streaming complexity characterizations for constraint satisfaction problems over arbitrary finite domains, using the notion of a core subrelation.
motivation: Streaming complexity of CSPs is a central problem in classical theoretical computer science, with prior characterizations limited to Boolean relations or specific objectives.
method: The authors reduce each CSP to its core, a canonical subrelation that admits gadgets for hard-pinning variables, and use this to design deterministic streaming algorithms and prove matching lower bounds.
result: They obtain tight characterizations (up to polylogarithmic factors, even against randomized algorithms) for satisfiability, approximate minimization of unsatisfied constraints, and exact maximum satisfiability on unweighted CSP instances over arbitrary finite domains.
conclusion: The core of a relation is shown to characterize the one-pass streaming complexity of CSPs in the general setting, resolving open cases left by previous work.

title: Understanding And Enhancing Backdoor Persistency In Llm Agent Post-Training
authors: Qiusi Zhan, Nian Lyu, Stephanie Ding, Arnav Mehta, Xander Davies, Daniel Kang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07510v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Developers can build LLM agents by adapting third-party models through benign post-training. We study a supply-chain threat in which an attacker supplies a model with a backdoor: hidden behavior that produces malicious outputs when a particular input pattern appears. Focusing on software-engineering agents, we ask whether such backdoors survive the developer's supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and subsequent task-level reinforcement learning (RL). We observe that benign SFT substantially reduces attack success, but subsequent RL often preserves the residual behavior and sometimes even increases attack success. Our analysis of backdoor erosion during SFT identifies two factors that may favor survival: initial backdoor strength and gradient compatibility with benign training. These factors motivate PersistBD, which refines an already-backdoored model before release to improve its persistency through the benign post-training process. On Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, PersistBD raises attack success from 20% to 74% after SFT and from 20% to 76% after SFT-RL, while maintaining comparable benign task performance. Together, our results show that backdoors can remain active through benign post-training and that adversaries can deliberately increase their persistence. This highlights a supply-chain risk for AI developers and motivates stronger techniques for detecting and mitigating inherited backdoors when adapting third-party models into agents. Our code is available at [URL].
tldr: This paper studies whether backdoors in LLM software-engineering agents survive benign supervised fine-tuning (SFT) and subsequent reinforcement learning (RL), and proposes PersistBD to deliberately increase backdoor persistence.
motivation: Attackers can supply third-party models with hidden backdoors, creating a supply-chain threat when developers adapt them into agents via benign post-training; it is unclear whether such backdoors survive the developer's SFT and RL.
method: The authors analyze backdoor erosion during SFT and identify initial backdoor strength and gradient compatibility with benign training as factors favoring survival, then introduce PersistBD to refine an already-backdoored model before release to improve persistency.
result: On Qwen2.5-Coder-7B, PersistBD raises attack success from 20% to 74% after SFT and from 20% to 76% after SFT-RL, while maintaining comparable benign task performance.
conclusion: Backdoors can remain active through benign post-training, and adversaries can deliberately increase their persistence; this highlights a supply-chain risk and motivates stronger detection and mitigation of inherited backdoors.

title: Bvi: Lightweight, Data-Centric Blockchain-Based Verification Of Identity Claims
authors: Harshith Pothapala, Gagandeep Singh, Samudi Amarasinghe, Priyanka Singh, Xue Li
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07531v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: A person who answers an unexpected call claiming to come from a bank has no way to check the claim. Australian text messaging has labelled a message as unverified when the sender identifier is not registered since 1 July 2026, but a voice call still arrives with nothing behind it, and voice cloning has removed the last cue recipients relied on. We present BVI, which answers one question for the recipient: did the calling party prove it holds a credential a registered organisation issued for this call? BVI keeps the organisational record, its authorised channels and its revocation state on a public ledger in a directly queryable form, and puts all decision logic in the handset, which performs eleven checks, pays no transaction fee and holds no full-chain state. We define ten attack classes plus the case in which revocation cannot be resolved, compare them in a 10-by-4 coverage matrix spanning BBCA, the content digest, the detector and composed BVI, and run 27 automated scenario tests against isolated Hardhat fixture states of the BVI contract; all 27 pass. For media substitution and synthetic speech, the contract tests validate commitment and gating properties rather than claiming detector accuracy. The mandatory per-session anchor costs about 91.5k gas and is invariant in call duration and hop count; each participating intermediary additionally contributes one optional attestation write. In a 20,000-session-per-cell path simulation, at one quarter carrier participation BVI detects 20.6 per cent of randomly located in-path rewrites versus 0.1 per cent for the every-hop comparison, while identity and content evidence remain available even when path evidence is indeterminate. We also quantify the throughput ceiling of the anchoring design.
tldr: BVI is a lightweight blockchain-based system for verifying that a voice caller holds a credential issued by a registered organization for that call.
motivation: Phone recipients cannot verify unexpected callers claiming to be from a bank, and voice cloning removes traditional audio cues; Australian text messaging has a verification label but voice calls lack such assurance.
method: BVI stores organizational records, authorized channels, and revocation state on a public ledger in queryable form, with all decision logic in the handset performing eleven checks; it defines ten attack classes and evaluates a 10x4 coverage matrix plus 27 automated Hardhat scenario tests.
result: All 27 contract scenario tests pass; the mandatory per-session anchor costs about 91.5k gas and is invariant in call duration and hop count, and in a 20,000-session-per-cell path simulation at one-quarter carrier participation BVI detects 20.6% of in-path rewrites versus 0.1% for every-hop comparison.
conclusion: BVI provides a practical, low-cost blockchain-based verification mechanism for identity claims in voice calls, with quantified attack coverage, gas costs, and throughput ceiling.

title: HarnessSecurity-Bench: Do Security Mechanisms Really Protect Coding Agent Harnesses?
authors: Zhengyang Zhu, Liming Huang, Runmin Ji, Mingxi Ye, Zihan Zhou, Hanyang Guo, Jingwen Wu, Yuhan Ye, Yuming Feng, Hong-Ning Dai, Zibin Zheng
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07639v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Coding agent harnesses mediate tool use and authorize actions, yet their security mechanisms and runtime effects remain incompletely characterized. We present HarnessSecurity, the first systematic empirical study and benchmark of open- and closed-source coding agent harnesses. First, we derive a ten-mechanism taxonomy and then assess 400 harness-mechanism cells using independent ratings by researchers and large language model (LLM) judges. We find that about half of confirmed mechanism implementations are opt-in, while closed-source harnesses exhibit substantial evidence gaps. Second, we introduce HarnessSecurity-Bench, a benchmark of 23 tasks across five attack surfaces without sacrificing legitimate task requirements. Using separate deterministic oracles to measure task utility and attack effects with security setting comparisons, we evaluate nine mechanisms across six leading harnesses: Claude Code, Codex CLI, Gemini CLI, gptme, Qwen Code, and GitHub Copilot. Under a controlled LLM baseline GLM-5.2, we conduct 2,500 trials, recording 81,155 tool calls and over 2.2 billion tokens. Enabling auto-approve increases utility and raises attack success from 29.2% to 95.6%. Network isolation and read-only mode reduce attack effects with substantial utility losses, while command allowlisting and command denylisting reduce attack effects with a small utility loss and a utility gain, respectively. Task-level cases show that restrictions on a shared capability can obstruct both legitimate and malicious operations, and that allowed tools or commands can leave unauthorized operations reachable through alternative execution paths. Harness providers should make security settings verifiable, test alternative execution paths to protected operations, and assess attack effects alongside task utility and execution costs.
tldr: A large-scale empirical benchmark evaluating whether security mechanisms in coding agent harnesses actually prevent attacks while preserving task utility.
motivation: Coding agent harnesses control tool use and authorization, but their security mechanisms and real-world effectiveness are poorly characterized, especially across open- and closed-source systems.
method: The authors derive a ten-mechanism taxonomy, rate 400 harness-mechanism cells, and introduce HarnessSecurity-Bench with 23 tasks across five attack surfaces. They evaluate nine security mechanisms across six harnesses using deterministic oracles for utility and attack effects in 2,500 trials.
result: Auto-approve raises attack success from 29.2% to 95.6% while increasing utility; network isolation and read-only mode reduce attacks but hurt utility; allowlisting and denylisting reduce attack effects with small utility loss or gain. Alternative execution paths can bypass restricted tools.
conclusion: Harness providers should make security settings verifiable, test alternative execution paths to protected operations, and assess attack effects alongside task utility and execution costs.

title: SkillPoison: Progressive Skill Poisoning Via Successful Experiences
authors: Lizhi Zhang, Xin He, Dianxuan Fu, Yuyuan Feng, Jiatong Li, Qi Wang, Xin Wang, Qinggang Zhang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07645v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Self-improving LLM agents increasingly distill successful experiences into persistent, reusable skills. Existing skill attack methods corrupt this learning pipeline by injecting malicious triggers, behaviors, or false facts into individual experiences or extracted skills. However, such attacks are easily detected, and the injected malicious behaviors often fail to accumulate as persistent skills. In this paper, we show that skill poisoning can arise even from verified successful experiences, without making any individual trajectory malicious. Based on this insight, we propose SkillPoison, a novel framework that progressively poisons skill via successful experiences. SkillPoison first constructs a set of successful experiences that reinforce a target behavior, and then removes the contextual conditions that constrain when the behavior applies. Rather than injecting malicious content, SkillPoison shapes how the skill extractor generalizes, allowing useful behavior to support task success while inducing harmful behavior when they are misapplied. Extensive experiments on three benchmarks show that SkillPoison achieves 95.71% attack success rates, while all injected experiences remain task-correct and pass verification and lexical inspection. Our code, data and implementation details are available for the community at [URL].
tldr: SkillPoison is an attack framework that progressively poisons reusable skills in self-improving LLM agents using only verified successful experiences.
motivation: Existing skill attacks on LLM agents inject malicious content that is easily detected and fails to persist; the authors investigate whether poisoning can arise from benign successful experiences.
method: SkillPoison constructs successful experiences that reinforce a target behavior, then removes contextual constraints to shape how the skill extractor generalizes, causing harmful misapplication.
result: The attack achieves 95.71% success across three benchmarks while all injected experiences remain task-correct and pass verification and lexical inspection.
conclusion: Skill poisoning can be a serious threat even without malicious-looking data, highlighting a vulnerability in skill distillation pipelines for LLM agents.

title: Lifecycle-Based Design And Evaluation Of Real-Time Backup Triggers For Ransomware Damage Mitigation
authors: Ryotaro Kobayashi Kosuke Higuchi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07854v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Ransomware continues to encrypt files during the interval between attack onset and detection. Real-time backups can mitigate this damage by preserving files before they are modified. The previously proposed Real-Time Open-File Backup System (ROFBS) triggers backups primarily on file-open events. However, the file lifecycle offers several candidate trigger points, including open, read, write, and rename operations. Triggering backups too early may create unnecessary backup files, whereas triggering them too late may allow ransomware writes to race with backup creation and prevent the preservation of clean file contents. Consequently, it remains unclear which trigger timing best balances recoverability and the number of backups created. In this study, we design and evaluate real-time backup triggers for mitigating ransomware damage from a file-lifecycle perspective. Specifically, we compare four strategies: Open-time backup, Read-time backup, Write-time backup, and Rename-time backup. We implement these strategies in an ROFBS-style prototype on XFS and evaluate them using five ransomware samples: Conti, Sodinokibi, AvosLocker, REvil, and HelloKitty. Our results clarify how trigger timing affects both damage mitigation and the number of backups created, providing design guidance for selecting effective triggers in real-time backup systems against ransomware.
tldr: The paper evaluates lifecycle-based real-time backup trigger strategies to mitigate ransomware damage.
motivation: Ransomware encrypts files before detection, and real-time backups can preserve clean file contents, but the optimal trigger timing remains unclear.
method: The authors compare open-time, read-time, write-time, and rename-time backup triggers in an ROFBS-style prototype on XFS using five ransomware samples.
result: The study clarifies how trigger timing affects both damage mitigation and the number of backups created.
conclusion: It provides design guidance for selecting effective triggers in real-time backup systems against ransomware.

title: On The Complexity Of Mixed Equilibria In First-Price Auctions With Correlated Priors
authors: Mark Chen, Xi Chen, Hao Cui, William Pires, Jonah Stockwell
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07858v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We show that computing an approximate mixed Bayes-Nash equilibrium in a discrete first-price auction with correlated priors is PPAD-complete. The key intermediate step in our reduction is the PPAD-completeness of computing an approximate Nash equilibrium in a new normal-form game, the hypergraph discrete first-price auction, which may be of independent interest.
tldr: The paper proves that computing an approximate mixed Bayes-Nash equilibrium in discrete first-price auctions with correlated priors is PPAD-complete.
motivation: Understanding the computational complexity of equilibrium computation in auctions with correlated priors is important for algorithmic game theory.
method: The authors give a reduction whose key intermediate step establishes PPAD-completeness for a new normal-form game, the hypergraph discrete first-price auction.
result: Computing an approximate mixed Bayes-Nash equilibrium in discrete first-price auctions with correlated priors is PPAD-complete.
conclusion: The work establishes computational intractability of equilibrium computation in this auction setting and introduces a new game class of independent interest.

title: The Amplifier Effect: Human-Factor Risks Of AI-Suggested Correlation And Auto-Propagation In Multi-Framework Grc Self-Assessment
authors: Nikolaos Kekatos, Michael Ioannou, Marina Korgiala-Karyda, Alexios Lekidis, Tom Nianios
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07866v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Multi-framework Governance, Risk and Compliance (GRC) platforms increasingly automate the link between an organisation's self-assessment answer and the compliance obligations that answer is said to satisfy. Cross-framework control mapping, AI-suggested question correlation, and automatic propagation of answers and evidence across correlated questions all serve the legitimate efficiency goal of reducing duplicate work for small and medium-sized enterprises under the EU Cyber Resilience Act, NIS2 and GDPR. The same mechanisms, however, amplify the consequences of any human-factor bias in a single answer: one optimistically-graded control, one rubber-stamped attestation, or one AI-drafted answer can be silently replicated as evidence of compliance with many obligations across multiple frameworks. We call this the amplifier effect: a platform-design property (coarse-grained attestation and un-gated propagation) rather than a failing of individual users. Using two EU-funded SME-facing GRC platforms, CYBERFORT and CYBER-BRIDGE, as examples, we (i) describe the amplification mechanism in concrete data-model terms, (ii) propose a six-dimension scoring framework for evaluating any GRC tool's exposure to the effect, (iii) instantiate the framework on a thirteen-tool comparison covering enterprise IRM, mid-market platforms, compliance-automation tools, and the two EU SME projects, and (iv) outline a measurement protocol that a consortium with access to production self-assessment data can run. The thirteen-tool comparison is a structured design assessment, not an empirical measurement of user behaviour. The EU SME platforms score lowest on the amplifier dimensions because their burden-reduction design deliberately trades sign-off granularity for throughput; we report this as a design trade-off, not a verdict on the platforms. Our contribution is the framing and the measurement protocol.
tldr: The paper identifies an 'amplifier effect' in multi-framework GRC platforms where AI-suggested correlations and auto-propagation can silently replicate human biases across compliance obligations, and proposes a scoring framework and measurement protocol.
motivation: Multi-framework Governance, Risk and Compliance platforms automate control mapping and answer propagation to reduce duplicate work for SMEs under EU regulations, but these same mechanisms may amplify the consequences of a single biased or optimistic self-assessment.
method: Using two EU-funded SME-facing GRC platforms as examples, the authors describe the amplification mechanism in data-model terms, propose a six-dimension scoring framework, instantiate it on a thirteen-tool comparison, and outline a measurement protocol for production self-assessment data.
result: The thirteen-tool comparison is a structured design assessment showing that the EU SME platforms score lowest on amplifier dimensions because their burden-reduction design trades sign-off granularity for throughput; this is reported as a design trade-off rather than a verdict.
conclusion: The paper's contribution is the framing of the amplifier effect and a measurement protocol, not an empirical study of user behavior; it highlights platform-design risks in AI-assisted compliance automation.

title: Dual-channel Metasurfaces For Refractometric And Spatial Heterogeneity Sensing
authors: Zhongjun Jiang, Nicolas Gomez, Soyaib H Sohag, You Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07188v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Nanophotonic sensors amplify analyte-induced optical signals through resonantly enhanced light-matter interactions. While effective for refractometric sensing, conventional sensing platforms typically collapse spatial variations in analyte distributions into ensemble-averaged readouts, thereby obscuring local heterogeneity. Here we present a dual-channel metasurface sensor capable of detecting both net analyte loading and nanoscale spatial inhomogeneity at deep-subwavelength scales. The device supports two distinct high-Q modes with deeply structured near-field profiles of opposite parity. Their complementary modal responses decouple analyte perturbations into bulk and differential components, which are encoded into two spectrally resolvable channels. We demonstrate these sensing modalities across analyte configurations exhibiting diverse forms of nanoscale heterogeneity, achieving a refractometric sensitivity of 357 nm/RIU and inhomogeneity detection below [MATH]. This dual-channel capability, which extends nanophotonic sensing from analyte quantity to its spatial variation, opens a new avenue for multidimensional analysis of biological and material systems.
tldr: A dual-channel metasurface sensor detects both net analyte loading and nanoscale spatial inhomogeneity in deep-subwavelength sensing.
motivation: Conventional nanophotonic sensors average spatial variations in analyte distributions, obscuring local heterogeneity and limiting multidimensional analysis.
method: The device supports two high-Q modes with opposite-parity near-field profiles, whose complementary responses decouple analyte perturbations into bulk and differential components encoded in two spectral channels.
result: It achieves refractometric sensitivity of 357 nm/RIU and enables inhomogeneity detection below deep-subwavelength scales across diverse analyte configurations.
conclusion: The dual-channel capability extends nanophotonic sensing from analyte quantity to spatial variation, opening avenues for biological and material analysis.

title: A Pressure-based Coupled General Synthetic Iterative Scheme For Rarefied Gas Flow Simulation
authors: Yanbing Zhang, Yifan Wen, Lei WU
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07658v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This work develops a pressure-based coupled (PBC) GSIS. Within each GSIS iteration, a conventional kinetic solver advances the velocity distribution function, from which non-equilibrium constitutive relations are extracted. A PBC macroscopic solver then solves the steady macroscopic synthetic equations: continuity and momentum equations are solved as a coupled pressure-velocity system under fixed temperature, followed by a segregated temperature solve. A boundary treatment is constructed to maintain strict consistency between kinetic boundary fluxes and macroscopic boundary conditions throughout the macroscopic iterations. The proposed method is validated against direct simulation Monte Carlo (DSMC) data across multiple three-dimensional test cases, including tube-to-vacuum flows, a dynamic gas lock configuration for EUV lithography, divertors in nuclear fusion, and sphere flow at Mach numbers up to 10. Numerical results demonstrate that our GSIS-PBC preserves asymptotic-preserving properties and yields satisfactory accuracy across continuum-to-transitional flow regimes. For low-speed near-continuum internal flows, GSIS-PBC delivers wall clock time speed-ups of up to two orders of magnitude compared with the conventional iterative scheme, and substantially outperforms the original density-based GSIS for challenging low-Mach internal flow problems. For nuclear-fusion divertor flows, GSIS-PBC is faster than the DSMC by four orders of magnitude.
tldr: A pressure-based coupled general synthetic iterative scheme (GSIS-PBC) is developed to accelerate rarefied gas flow simulations across continuum-to-transitional regimes.
motivation: Conventional kinetic solvers for rarefied gas flows are computationally expensive, especially in low-Mach near-continuum regimes, motivating faster macroscopic-kinetic hybrid methods.
method: Within each GSIS iteration a kinetic solver advances the velocity distribution function to extract non-equilibrium constitutive relations, while a pressure-based macroscopic solver handles steady continuity and momentum equations as a coupled pressure-velocity system plus a segregated temperature solve, with consistent kinetic-macroscopic boundary treatment.
result: Validated against DSMC across 3D test cases (tube-to-vacuum flow, EUV lithography gas lock, fusion divertors, sphere flow up to Mach 10), GSIS-PBC achieves up to two orders of magnitude speed-up over conventional iterative schemes and four orders of magnitude over DSMC for divertor flows.
conclusion: The scheme preserves asymptotic-preserving properties and delivers accurate, substantially faster solutions for rarefied gas flows, particularly outperforming density-based GSIS in low-Mach internal flows.

title: Linear Occupancy Homomorphisms For Discounted Markov Decision Processes
authors: Sarah H. Q. Li Yihan Liu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07441v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We introduce linear occupancy homomorphisms (LOHs), a class of Markov decision process (MDP) transformations that defines the MDP homomorphism over the feasible occupancy measure space of MDPs. In contrast to classic MDP homomorphism frameworks, which are defined through mappings over the state and state-action spaces, LOHs map between occupancy measure spaces and are representable as linear transformation matrices that expose important structural properties of the homomorphism itself. For this class of MDP transformations, we derive finite dimensional linear inequality constraints that certify when a candidate transformation matrix is a valid LOH and derive the corresponding transformed MDP. We further establish a connection between LOHs, soft MDP homomorphisms, and factored matrix robust MDPs. When the linear transformation matrix is invertible, we prove that the original MDP is equivalent to a constrained MDP after the homomorphic transformation, and derive necessary and sufficient conditions under which the LOH preserves the optimal value. We illustrate the benefits of LOHs in two settings: improving robust MDP solutions by transforming nonrectangular parameter uncertainty sets into homomorphic rectangular MDPs, and decomposing a large MDP into smaller independent MDPs.
tldr: The paper introduces linear occupancy homomorphisms, a class of linear transformations between the occupancy-measure spaces of Markov decision processes, and characterizes when such a transformation preserves optimal value or yields equivalent constrained MDPs.
motivation: Classical MDP homomorphisms are defined via mappings on state and state-action spaces, which obscures structural properties; the authors seek a formulation directly over occupancy measures that exposes the algebraic structure of the transformation.
method: They define linear occupancy homomorphisms as linear transformation matrices acting on occupancy-measure spaces, derive finite-dimensional linear inequality constraints certifying validity, and relate the framework to soft MDP homomorphisms and factored matrix robust MDPs.
result: For invertible transformation matrices they prove equivalence between the original MDP and a constrained MDP after transformation and give necessary and sufficient conditions for optimal-value preservation, illustrating gains in robust MDP solving and MDP decomposition.
conclusion: LOHs provide a linear-algebraic lens on MDP abstraction that improves robust MDP solutions by rectifying nonrectangular uncertainty sets and enables decomposition of large MDPs into smaller independent ones.

title: Tare: Weigh A Never-Poisoned Twin Before Reading Backdoor-Defense Costs
authors: Ruizhi Xu, Wei Xu, Sibo Zhu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.06994v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Backdoor-defense leaderboards print a clean-accuracy drop and read it as removal cost. Measured on the poisoned victim alone, the drop cannot separate removal from what the defense does to any model, and inherits the victim's start, which for three of BackdoorBench's sixteen attacks is a configuration file: WaNet, BPP and Input-Aware ship a MultiStepLR that never fires, so their victims never anneal and are the least accurate in 30/31 public CIFAR cells at [MATH]5%. On PreAct-ResNet18, fine-tuning-family defenses return a low start to their own level, so there the published cost is negative, the benchmark's rating clips the "gain" to zero, and 2 of 48 citing defense papers we read rest a no-cost claim on those cells; TSBD and CGD, re-run with their code, "gain" on a never-poisoned model too. A [MATH] editing only that scheduler line isolates the cause, its swapped arms self-registered before they ran: the sign of the fine-tuning family's clean-model cost reverses both ways while its published gain on the annealed victim only shrinks toward zero, 44/44 seeds following the schedule, replicated on BPP, FT-SAM, CIFAR-100 and VGG19-BN and induced in a second toolkit. TARE runs the same defense on a never-poisoned twin of the same recipe, schedule and seed (on BackdoorBench, [MATH]10 poisoned images, admitted only below 5% attack success); what the twin loses is the tare. On the BadNets grid seven of eight defenses charge the twin (Neural Cleanse only where its detector fires), +0.13 (fine-tuning) to +5.70 points (I-BAU); the eighth, ABL, destroys it. Within an attack the start cancels from rankings, so the tare re-orders nothing there; what poisoning adds beyond it is printed under two estimators and not corrected, its removal share unidentified. We ship the three-key patch, a signed tare column (7 attacks [MATH] 8 defenses) and TARE-Z, a twin-free estimator for seed-stable defenses.
tldr: The paper diagnoses a benchmark flaw in backdoor-defense evaluation, where reported clean-accuracy drops conflate defense-induced degradation with poisoning-removal cost, and proposes a TARE twin-estimator to isolate removal cost.
motivation: Backdoor-defense leaderboards interpret clean-accuracy drops on poisoned models as removal cost, but this fails to distinguish actual backdoor removal from a defense's generic effect on any model, and can be distorted by victim initialization or scheduler artifacts.
method: The authors analyze BackdoorBench and show that certain attacks ship non-firing learning-rate schedulers, then introduce TARE, which runs the same defense on a never-poisoned twin of the same recipe, schedule, and seed, and measures what the twin loses as the tare cost.
result: On BadNets, seven of eight defenses charge the never-poisoned twin, with costs from +0.13 to +5.70 points, while ABL destroys it; the sign of the fine-tuning family's clean-model cost reverses under a scheduler edit, and published gains only shrink toward zero.
conclusion: Backdoor-defense leaderboards should report a signed tare column to separate removal cost from generic defense cost, and TARE-Z provides a twin-free estimator for seed-stable defenses.

title: Jailbreaking Open-Weight LLMs Via Random Embedding Perturbations
authors: Abhinav Sudhakar Dubey (university Of California Santa Cruz), Scott Sirri (university Of California Santa Cruz), Vaggos Chatziafratis (university Of California Santa Cruz), C. Seshadhri
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07125v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: While open-weight models have enjoyed steady progress in capabilities and wide adoption across multiple domains, their safety remains an important concern. One key feature is the ability to refuse or deflect harmful, malicious, or insensitive prompts. In this paper, we expose safety vulnerabilities across six common open-weight LLMs of various sizes that consistently lead to harmful or unsafe responses on the JailbreakBench benchmark dataset. Our proposed attack, Perturbed Embedding Vector (PEV), is a simple and fast "jailbreaking" technique that is cheaper than prior approaches, which typically require gradient computations, per-prompt optimizations, or altering internal weights of the models. PEV just adds independent Gaussian noise in the embedding vector representations of the prompt, with no need for further manipulations. To generate unsafe responses, we repeatedly sample additive noise from this distribution. In our experiments, we observe that the average compute cost to get the first successful attack is up to an order of magnitude less than previous attacks. The first successful jailbreak on a new prompt typically arrives within one minute on every tested model, and PEV generates unsafe responses across all models for all prompts in JailbreakBench. No other tested method achieves such results, despite them taking longer to run. More broadly, we believe that understanding the behavior of LLMs under perturbations in the embedding vectors is an important research direction: while perturbations constitute a major security risk, they can also serve as a valuable tool for exploring the dynamical behavior of such models.
tldr: The paper introduces Perturbed Embedding Vector (PEV), a cheap jailbreaking attack that adds random Gaussian noise to prompt embeddings of open-weight LLMs to elicit harmful responses.
motivation: Open-weight LLMs remain vulnerable to jailbreaks, and existing attacks often require expensive gradient computations, per-prompt optimization, or weight modifications.
method: PEV repeatedly samples independent Gaussian noise and adds it directly to the prompt embedding representations, avoiding gradients, weight changes, or further manipulations.
result: Across six open-weight LLMs and JailbreakBench prompts, PEV achieves the first successful attack within about one minute and up to an order of magnitude lower compute than prior methods, ultimately generating unsafe responses for all tested prompts and models.
conclusion: Embedding perturbations are a practical security risk and also a useful tool for probing the dynamical behavior of LLMs, motivating further study of robustness under embedding-space noise.

title: Leo Signals-of-Opportunity For Navigation In Urban Environments: A GLRT-Assisted Off-Grid Sbl Approach
authors: Maedeh Sotoodenia, Mohammad Hossein Kahaei, Alireza Nezamalhosseini
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07871v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The vulnerability and unavailability of global navigation satellite system (GNSS) signals in dense urban environments have motivated the use of low earth orbit (LEO) signals of opportunity (SoOP) for positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT). However, multipath and non-ideal noise can significantly degrade delay--Doppler estimation and, consequently, navigation accuracy. This paper proposes a hybrid generalized likelihood ratio test (GLRT) and off-grid sparse Bayesian learning (SBL) framework for LEO-SoOP navigation under multipath and non-Gaussian, temporally correlated noise. First, a GLRT-based framework is developed, demonstrating reliable detection under ideal Gaussian noise but degraded estimation under heavy-tailed or colored noise and unresolved multipath. Next, an off-grid SBL framework is introduced for high-resolution separation and estimation of line-of-sight (LOS) delay--Doppler parameters. The estimated LOS parameters are subsequently tracked and incorporated into an extended Kalman filter (EKF) to obtain the navigation solution. Simulation results demonstrate that, in urban environments, the proposed method reduces delay RMSE by up to 77\% and position RMSE by 88.5\% compared with GLRT-based estimation. These results demonstrate the potential of the proposed framework for robust and accurate LEO-SoOP navigation.
tldr: The paper proposes a hybrid GLRT and off-grid sparse Bayesian learning framework for LEO signals-of-opportunity navigation in urban environments under multipath and non-Gaussian noise.
motivation: GNSS signals are unreliable in dense urban settings, motivating the use of low Earth orbit signals of opportunity for positioning, navigation, and timing, but multipath and non-ideal noise degrade delay-Doppler estimation.
method: A GLRT detection framework is first developed, then an off-grid SBL framework performs high-resolution separation and estimation of line-of-sight delay-Doppler parameters, which are tracked with an extended Kalman filter to produce the navigation solution.
result: Simulations show reductions of up to 77% in delay RMSE and 88.5% in position RMSE compared with GLRT-based estimation in urban environments.
conclusion: The proposed GLRT-assisted off-grid SBL approach offers robust and accurate LEO-SoOP navigation, though it lies entirely outside quantum information science.

title: Preparing An AI-Augmented Siem For The Eu Cyber Resilience Act: A Practitioner Case Study
authors: Georgios Koutidis, Nikolaos Kekatos, Marina Korgiala-Karyda, Alexios Lekidis, Tom Nianios
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07873v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The EU Cyber Resilience Act (CRA), Regulation (EU) 2024/2847, makes product cybersecurity a lifecycle obligation for products with digital elements on the EU market: risk assessment, vulnerability handling, conformity documentation, and Article 14 incident- and vulnerability-reporting readiness must be operational before market placement. Small and medium-sized enterprises that build security products are doubly exposed, since their products are in scope while their customers expect them to be exemplary. This case study documents a CRA preparedness pilot for one such product, SEUXDR, an AI-augmented security monitoring product with a large-language-model active-response component, on the open-source CYBERFORT platform. We contribute a reproducible six-step recipe (Scope and Classify, Asset Registration, Produce Evidence, Map to CRA, Gap and Actions, Audit Pack), two end-to-end traceability threads, and a pilot snapshot tracing product risks through baseline and AI-specific controls and policies to CRA objectives. It offers practitioners a replicable starting point for translating CRA legal text into operational preparedness for incident response, vulnerability reporting, and conformity assessment.
tldr: This practitioner case study documents a CRA preparedness pilot for an AI-augmented security monitoring product (SEUXDR) on the open-source CYBERFORT platform, offering a reproducible six-step recipe for translating EU Cyber Resilience Act legal requirements into operational readiness.
motivation: The EU Cyber Resilience Act (Regulation (EU) 2024/2847) imposes lifecycle cybersecurity obligations on products with digital elements, and small and medium-sized enterprises building security products are doubly exposed because their own products are in scope while customers expect exemplary compliance.
method: The authors conduct a case study pilot for the SEUXDR product, defining a reproducible six-step recipe (Scope and Classify, Asset Registration, Produce Evidence, Map to CRA, Gap and Actions, Audit Pack), two end-to-end traceability threads, and a pilot snapshot linking product risks through baseline and AI-specific controls and policies to CRA objectives.
result: The pilot yields a traceable mapping from product risks and AI-specific controls to CRA objectives for incident response, vulnerability reporting, and conformity assessment, providing evidence artifacts and audit-pack documentation.
conclusion: The paper offers practitioners a replicable starting point for operationalizing CRA legal text into preparedness processes, though it is a compliance/security-engineering case study with no connection to quantum information, thermodynamics, quantum networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Calibration-Free Broadband Reconstructive Spectrometer Based On Conical Phase Modulation
authors: Junrui Liang, Zhongming Huang, Yanting Guo, Jun Ye, Yanzhao Ke, Jun Li, Jiangming Xu, Jinyong Leng, Pu Zhou
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07021v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reconstructive spectrometers (RSs) shift spectral analysis from hardware-heavy dispersion to encoding-decoding schemes. In the speckle-based RSs, spectra are encoded into disordered intensity patterns and then recovered algorithmically. However, characterizing such spectral-encoding transmission matrices (TMs) typically demands empirically complex calibrations, which rely on expensive tunable light sources to generate known wavelengths. In this work, we demonstrate a fully calibration-free RS that leverages conical phase modulation from an axicon. The target spectra are encoded into a Bessel-form intensity profile, enabling computational construction of a deterministic TM and thus completely removing the need for optical calibration. With this computer-generated TM, broadband spectral reconstruction is experimentally achieved across a 650 nm range (1050-1700 nm)--nearly three times the bandwidth of existing calibration-simplified RSs--while a spectral resolution of 2.9 nm remains comparable to that of these counterparts. Compared with an RS requiring optical calibration for equivalent performance, our solution achieves an approximate 36-fold cost reduction.Unlike most speckle RSs, the axicon RS requires no fixed input polarizer, further enhancing energy efficiency and simplicity through polarization-insensitive operation. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first reported experimentally calibration-free RS, featuring superior simplicity, practicality, and cost-effectiveness for practical applications.
tldr: A calibration-free broadband reconstructive spectrometer using an axicon-induced conical phase modulation to generate a deterministic transmission matrix for spectral reconstruction.
motivation: Speckle-based reconstructive spectrometers typically require complex and expensive optical calibration with known tunable light sources, limiting practicality and increasing cost.
method: The authors encode target spectra into a Bessel-form intensity profile via conical phase modulation from an axicon, enabling computational construction of a deterministic transmission matrix without optical calibration.
result: The device experimentally reconstructs spectra over a 650 nm range (1050–1700 nm) with 2.9 nm resolution, achieving about 36-fold cost reduction and polarization-insensitive operation.
conclusion: This is the first experimental demonstration of a fully calibration-free reconstructive spectrometer, offering simplicity, practicality, and cost-effectiveness for broadband spectral analysis.

title: The Search Process Of Professional Detection Dog Teams In Realistic Environments
authors: Stephan P. Kaufhold, Jack Terwilliger, Samantha Kefer, Federico Rossano
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07129v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Scent detection work is a form of interspecies cooperation. Dogs sample odors that handlers cannot perceive, and handlers decide where the team searches and which of the dogs' responses counts as a find. However, detection performance is predominantly measured by outcomes and dog characteristics. To better observe the search process itself, we collected data at two judged detection events (109 searches of 37 professional narcotics teams). All searches were video-recorded and included an outdoor area, a vehicle, and a building search, each with two targets and food and currency distractors. We synchronized computer-vision tracking of dogs and handlers with continuous behavioral coding. We observed variation across teams and in total 42\% of targets were found. Finds were rarely missed because dogs never came close to a target or because handlers did not call an indication. Rather, most were missed at the encounter itself, as dogs came within 1~m of nearly every target but indicated on only about one in six of these passes. Handlers did not behave differently near targets than near distractors before their dogs responded. Finding targets was moderately consistent within teams, whereas false calls depended on the individual search and on specific items. Observing the search process suggests that success is a result of the dog's response, the handler's decision, and their coordination.
tldr: A behavioral study using computer-vision tracking and behavioral coding to characterize the search process of professional narcotics detection dog teams, finding that most missed targets stem from the dog failing to indicate despite coming within 1 m of the target.
motivation: Detection performance is typically measured only by outcomes and dog characteristics, so the actual search process involving dog-handler coordination remains poorly understood.
method: Video recordings of 109 searches by 37 professional narcotics teams across outdoor, vehicle, and building scenarios were analyzed by synchronizing computer-vision tracking of dogs and handlers with continuous behavioral coding.
result: Only 42% of targets were found; misses rarely resulted from dogs not approaching a target or handlers failing to call an indication, but rather from dogs indicating on only about one in six passes within 1 m of a target, while handlers behaved similarly near targets and distractors.
conclusion: Detection success emerges from the interaction of the dog's response, the handler's decision, and their coordination, rather than from dog capability or handler judgment alone.

title: Characteristics Of Extinction Behavior Of Ammonia Partial Cracking Simulated Fuels In Counterflow Premixed Flames Under Lean Condition
authors: Jinseong Kim, Hyunchang Lee, Keeman Lee, Assaad R. Masri
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07605v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this study, the lean extinction behaviors of CH4 and a 16% cracked ammonia surrogate fuel, CR16, in counterflow premixed flames were compared. Experiments were conducted along with one-dimensional simulations using OPPDIF; the GRI-Mech 3.0 and UCSD mechanisms were applied to CH4 and CR16, respectively. CR16 exhibited higher extinction strain rates and resilience to strain-induced blow-out (RSIB) than those of CH4 under lean conditions. At Phi = 0.66, although both flames had the same extinction strain rate, CR16 showed a higher RSIB because of its longer flame time. Near its extinction, CR16 sustained H2 consumption, radical reactions, and heat release through the interflame region toward the stagnation plane. Hydrogen oxidation coupled with nitrogen-related pathways, including NH2 + NO and HNO reactions, supported this behavior. These results clarify the chemical basis for the superior extinction resistance of economically favorable low-cracking-ratio ammonia fuel.
tldr: The paper experimentally and numerically compares lean extinction behavior of methane and a 16% cracked ammonia surrogate fuel in counterflow premixed flames, identifying chemical pathways that enhance extinction resistance.
motivation: Ammonia is an economically favorable carbon-free fuel, but its combustion stability under lean conditions needs improvement; partial cracking to hydrogen may enhance resilience to strain-induced blow-out.
method: Counterflow premixed flame experiments were combined with one-dimensional OPPDIF simulations using GRI-Mech 3.0 for CH4 and UCSD mechanism for the cracked ammonia surrogate CR16, focusing on extinction strain rates and radical pathways near extinction.
result: CR16 exhibited higher extinction strain rates and greater resilience to strain-induced blow-out than CH4 under lean conditions; at Φ=0.66 it showed longer flame time, sustained H2 consumption, radical reactions, and heat release through the interflame region, supported by NH2 + NO and HNO pathways.
conclusion: The superior extinction resistance of low-cracking-ratio ammonia fuel is chemically explained, supporting its use as an economically favorable lean-burn fuel.

title: A Mathematical Analogy Between Certain Hollow Vortex And Bubble Flows - Existence, Uniqueness, And Identical Boundary Shapes
authors: Valentin D. Kunz, Saleh Tanveer, Darren G. Crowdy
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07709v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study two physically distinct steady free-boundary problems in a two-dimensional inviscid fluid: a hollow vortex in a constant-vorticity flow subject to simple shear, third order and linear strain at infinity, without surface tension, and an irrotational flow past a constant-pressure bubble subject to surface tension, linear strain, and circulation at infinity. Building on the mathematical vortex-bubble correspondence recently developed by Crowdy and Tanveer, we show that both problems are linked by a common mathematical formulation. For the vortex problem, we extend the sequence-space fixed-point approach of Crowdy and Tanveer to obtain new local existence, uniqueness, and analyticity results. For the bubble problem, we develop a separate existence theory, reducing it to a nonlinear singular integral operator fixed-point problem and deriving a scalar solvability condition that defines a realanalytic surface in the physical parameter space. On this surface we obtain locally unique bubble solutions with real-analytic boundaries and holomorphically extendible velocity fields. Finally, we prove that the scalar solvability condition is equivalent to a functional conformal mapping identity. The scalar condition between the parameters is enough for the vortex and bubble problems to have the same free-boundary shape, despite their different exterior flows.
tldr: This paper establishes a mathematical analogy between two free-boundary fluid problems—a hollow vortex in shear flow and a bubble with surface tension—showing they share identical boundary shapes under a scalar solvability condition.
motivation: The authors aim to extend a recently developed vortex-bubble correspondence by Crowdy and Tanveer to include shear and strain at infinity, providing rigorous existence and uniqueness results for both problems.
method: They use sequence-space fixed-point methods for the vortex problem and reduce the bubble problem to a nonlinear singular integral operator fixed-point problem, deriving a scalar solvability condition that defines a real-analytic surface in parameter space.
result: Local existence, uniqueness, and analyticity are proven for both problems; the scalar condition is shown to be equivalent to a functional conformal mapping identity, and identical free-boundary shapes arise despite different exterior flows.
conclusion: The work deepens the mathematical understanding of a vortex-bubble analogy, providing rigorous tools for free-boundary problems in inviscid fluid dynamics.

title: Absolute Marchaud Integrability Is Not Necessary For Membership In Riemann--Liouville $L^p$ Images
authors: Salaheddine Lamzib, Aadil Lahrouz, Ahmed Zeghal
abstract: ArXiv:2610.06867v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: For every fractional order strictly between zero and one and every finite interval, there is a bounded representing function whose Riemann--Liouville fractional integral satisfies the weighted endpoint condition proposed by Vainikko but fails the absolute Marchaud condition almost everywhere. One bounded example therefore disproves the necessity implication in Vainikko's conjectured characterization simultaneously for every exponent strictly larger than one, including the essentially bounded endpoint. A different sine-series construction gives, at each exponent strictly between one and infinity, failure at every interior point for one representative. For the bounded example, signed inversion remains valid for every finite exponent greater than or equal to one. The converse implication in Vainikko's conjecture is not decided here.
tldr: The paper disproves a necessity implication in Vainikko's conjectured characterization of Riemann-Liouville L^p images by constructing bounded functions that fail the absolute Marchaud condition almost everywhere.
motivation: Vainikko conjectured a characterization of Riemann-Liouville fractional integral images in L^p spaces using a weighted endpoint condition and the absolute Marchaud condition. The necessity of the Marchaud condition was open.
method: The authors construct a bounded representing function for every fractional order in (0,1) and every finite interval, showing that its Riemann-Liouville fractional integral satisfies Vainikko's weighted endpoint condition but fails the absolute Marchaud condition almost everywhere. They also provide a sine-series construction for interior-point failure.
result: A single bounded example disproves the necessity implication for all exponents greater than one, including the essentially bounded case. The sine-series construction yields failure at every interior point for one representative at each exponent in (1,∞). Signed inversion remains valid for finite exponents ≥ 1.
conclusion: The necessity direction of Vainikko's conjecture is false, while the converse implication remains undecided. The results advance the theory of Riemann-Liouville fractional integral operators in L^p spaces.

title: Optimal Linear Functional Estimation For Proportionally High-Dimensional Linear Models
authors: Junwei Lu
abstract: ArXiv:2610.06875v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We study estimation of a linear functional in random-design linear models when [MATH] under the dense regime where the design covariance is unknown, and neither the regression vector nor the precision matrix is assumed sparse. Suppose the spectrum of the design covariance belongs to [MATH], we establish the minimax mean squared rate for the linear functional has the order [MATH], where the exponent [MATH] has an explicit elliptic-integral representation and [MATH] when both [MATH] and [MATH]. We propose the Bocca estimator, which combines empirically calibrated resolvents through a complex contour integral to attain the optimal rate.
tldr: The paper studies minimax optimal estimation of a linear functional in high-dimensional random-design linear models under dense, unknown-covariance regimes.
motivation: Estimating linear functionals in high-dimensional linear models is challenging when neither the regression vector nor the precision matrix is sparse and the design covariance is unknown.
method: The authors characterize the minimax mean squared error rate in terms of an elliptic-integral exponent and propose the Bocca estimator, which combines empirically calibrated resolvents via a complex contour integral.
result: They establish the minimax optimal rate for the linear functional and show the Bocca estimator attains this rate.
conclusion: The work provides optimal estimation theory for dense high-dimensional linear functionals, extending understanding beyond sparse regimes.

title: Economic Resources, Sporting Efficiency And Uncertainty: A Stochastic Optimization Model Of Football Performance In Africa
authors: Babacar Mbaye Ndiaye Thierno Thioune
abstract: ArXiv:2610.06967v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: We propose a stochastic optimization framework in which football performance is modeled as the result of an efficiency-driven production process under uncertainty. The model incorporates economic inputs, a latent efficiency variable evolving according to a stochastic differential equation, and a control variable representing investment in sports development. We derive the associated discounted Hamilton--Jacobi--Bellman (HJB) equation, characterize the optimal investment policy, prove a verification theorem under explicit growth conditions, and show that a bounded investment budget is required for the control problem to be well posed. We relate our efficiency measure to the stochastic frontier and data envelopment analysis (SFA/DEA) traditions used elsewhere in sports economics, and clarify what a dynamic control formulation adds relative to those static approaches. The theoretical results are illustrated with a numerical solution of the HJB equation -- validated by a grid-refinement convergence study -- and Monte Carlo simulations. A cross-sectional analysis of the 24 AFCON 2025 national teams, based on GDP, population, and FIFA ranking data, estimates country-specific conditional log-efficiency residuals using heteroskedasticity-robust inference. We show that these residuals are mechanically and strongly correlated with FIFA points by construction, quantify this dependence, and interpret the results accordingly. Teams such as Senegal and Morocco consistently outperform their GDP-implied potential, whereas others, including South Africa and Tanzania, tend to underperform. While these patterns are broadly consistent with observed AFCON outcomes, the estimated residual also captures unobserved factors, such as institutional quality, diaspora talent, and demographic structure, that are not included in the model.
tldr: The paper develops a stochastic optimal control model for football performance, linking economic inputs and latent efficiency to optimal investment under uncertainty.
motivation: The authors aim to move beyond static efficiency measures such as stochastic frontier analysis and data envelopment analysis by introducing a dynamic control formulation for sports performance.
method: They formulate an efficiency-driven production process with a latent efficiency variable following a stochastic differential equation and a control variable for sports investment, derive the Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman equation, prove a verification theorem, and estimate conditional log-efficiency residuals for AFCON 2025 teams using GDP, population, and FIFA ranking data.
result: The model yields optimal investment policy conditions, requires a bounded investment budget for well-posedness, and shows that country-specific residuals are mechanically correlated with FIFA points; Senegal and Morocco outperform GDP-implied potential while South Africa and Tanzania underperform.
conclusion: The dynamic control framework complements static SFA/DEA approaches, but the estimated residuals capture unobserved factors such as institutional quality, diaspora talent, and demographics, leaving broader interpretation cautionary.

title: Optimization By Reparametrization: Time-Warped Mirror Flows With Singular Geometry
authors: Cristian Vega, Cesare Molinari, Lorenzo Rosasco, Silvia Villa
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07040v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Solving data-driven problems requires defining complex models and fitting them to data, neural networks being a motivating example. The fitting procedure can be seen as an optimization problem, which is often non-convex, and hence optimization guarantees are hard to derive. An opportunity is provided by viewing the model of interest as a redundant reparameterization--an overparameterization--of some simpler model for which optimization results are easier to achieve. In this paper, after formalizing the above idea, we revisit some recent results and derive new ones. In particular, we consider the gradient flow of some classes of linear overparameterizations and show that they correspond to suitable mirror flows on the original parameters. Our main contribution relates to the study of the latter, for which we establish well-posedness and convergence. Several specific instances are provided, including fully connected linear networks and networks with weight normalization. The results yield insight into the role of overparameterization in optimization and corresponding implicit regularization properties.
tldr: The paper studies time-warped mirror flows arising from gradient flows of linear overparameterizations, establishing well-posedness and convergence while providing insight into implicit regularization in optimization.
motivation: Optimization of non-convex models like neural networks is difficult to analyze directly, so the authors leverage overparameterization to connect the dynamics to more tractable mirror flows on the original parameters.
method: They formalize redundant reparameterization, analyze gradient flows of linear overparameterizations, and show equivalence to mirror flows, proving well-posedness and convergence for several instances including fully connected linear networks and weight normalization.
result: The gradient flows of certain linear overparameterizations correspond to mirror flows with time warping, and convergence guarantees are established for these flows.
conclusion: The work clarifies how overparameterization influences optimization and yields implicit regularization properties, offering a theoretical framework for analyzing redundant parameterizations.

title: Model-Based Galerkin Lifting With Exact Lti Decomposition For Guaranteed $\mathcal{H}_\infty$ Output Feedback Control Of Nonlinear Systems
authors: Burak Kurkcu, Christopher Phan, Aleksandar Zecevic, Maryam Khanbaghi
abstract: ArXiv:2610.07299v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In this paper, we present a model-based Galerkin framework for output-feedback control of nonlinear systems with known dynamics. With a suitable actuator augmentation, the finite-dimensional realization preserves the actuator dynamics and the constant input matrix. We retain finite-order nonclosure as an explicit additive residual. The LTI part and this residual describe the lifted nonlinear dynamics exactly. The decomposition does not require an invariant subspace of observables and also applies to non-control-affine systems. We use regional bounds on the closure residual, actuator-realization defect, and output-reconstruction error in the standard [MATH] design. The proposed controller is a linear dynamic system driven only by the measured tracking error and requires no online lifting. Retaining the state coordinates gives direct bounds on the original state. We use these bounds to derive an a priori containment condition. Under this condition, the nonlinear closed loop is forward complete, and the state and tracking error satisfy explicit transient bounds and are uniformly ultimately bounded. The cart-pendulum example illustrates the nonlinear closed-loop guarantees and compares the controller with full-state backstepping. Although the output-feedback controller uses only the measured tracking error, it achieves almost the same nominal tracking RMSE as backstepping, with a lower peak tracking error.
tldr: A model-based Galerkin lifting framework with exact LTI decomposition for guaranteed H-infinity output feedback control of known nonlinear systems.
motivation: Nonlinear output feedback control with guaranteed performance is challenging, especially when nonlinearities are not control-affine and only output measurements are available.
method: The paper augments actuators and uses Galerkin lifting to exactly decompose nonlinear dynamics into an LTI part plus a finite-order closure residual, then designs a linear dynamic output-feedback controller using regional bounds on residual, actuator defect, and reconstruction error.
result: The controller yields a forward-complete closed loop with explicit transient bounds and uniform ultimate boundedness; on a cart-pendulum example it achieves tracking RMSE comparable to full-state backstepping with lower peak error.
conclusion: The proposed approach provides theoretical guarantees for output-feedback control of known nonlinear systems without online lifting, though it is unrelated to quantum information, thermodynamics, networks, or hybrid quantum systems.

title: Axiom Satisfiability Of Linear Rewards In Alignment
authors: Soumya Nasipuri, Sayak Ray Chowdhury, Sanjukta Roy
abstract: ArXiv:2610.06892v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Learning from human preference data is the dominant route to aligning language models with human values. In linear social choice, where rewards are linear in a fixed feature representation of prompt-response pairs, Ge et al.[2024] show that fitting such a reward by minimizing any non-decreasing convex loss, including BTL, fails PO and PMC. Moreover, no rule that reads only the majority relation can satisfy PO once the output is required to be linearly induced. We ask what it costs to enforce these axioms anyway. To this end, we relax the linear model to allow per-candidate slack. We compute the relaxed linear reward with the smallest total slack that satisfies the axioms with a margin [MATH], the minimum required difference between two reward values. Our solution satisfies the axioms under no assumptions about the voters or how comparisons were collected. We bound the optimal total slack by [MATH] when [MATH] is at most [MATH] for [MATH] candidates. Furthermore, we exhibit an instance that forces this bound, concluding that the rate is tight up to constants. In practice, the no. of candidates far exceeds the feature dimension, and only a linear reward can be evaluated on unseen responses. We therefore introduce a new method that charges the linear part for each comparison it gets wrong. It simultaneously minimizes the total slack and the no. of violations, with a parameter [MATH] trading off between them. We show that the total slack is monotone but saturating in [MATH]: raising it reduces the violations of the deployed linear reward and increases the slack, yet the slack stays below [MATH], where [MATH] and [MATH] are the diameter and dimension of the features, respectively. Experiments on both synthetic and real-life preference data corroborate our theory and show that the linear reward output by our method beats linear BTL.
tldr: This paper studies the cost of enforcing social choice axioms in linear reward models for aligning language models with human preferences.
motivation: Learning from human preference data via linear rewards can fail to satisfy desirable social choice axioms such as Pareto optimality and population monotonicity, raising the question of how much slack is needed to enforce them.
method: The authors relax the linear reward model with per-candidate slack, compute the minimal total slack satisfying axioms with a margin, bound it, and introduce a method trading off slack against violations.
result: They derive tight bounds on the optimal total slack and show that the slack is monotone but saturating in a trade-off parameter, with experiments confirming that the method outperforms linear BTL.
conclusion: The work provides a principled relaxation of linear reward models to satisfy alignment axioms, with theoretical bounds and practical benefits for preference learning.

title: Apex: Active Protection At Execution Boundaries For Llm Agents
authors: Xinran Zheng, Xin Fan Guo, Zhiqiang Hao, Fan Yang, Xingzhi Qian, Jiawei Du, Jinfeng Xu, Zheng Xing, Shuo Yang, Xingjun Wang
abstract: ArXiv:2610.06966v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Indirect prompt injection (IPI) hides adversarial instructions in content that large language model (LLM) agents read at runtime. As agents compose heterogeneous capability units, including Tools, MCP servers, and Skills, the carriers of injection multiply, and defenses built to recognize attack patterns fall behind them. We instead shift defense from covering attack patterns to one stable point: whatever the carrier and however the injection propagates, harm materializes only at the , where the agent turns internal state into an external action or released output. Safety there turns on two conditions, both settled by the trusted task rather than by the run: whether the proposed effect is authorized, and whether the runtime information reaching it is endorsed by that task. We present APEX, an active defense that enforces both at this boundary from a single authorization contract compiled before untrusted execution: admits an effect only when the contract justifies it, while makes unendorsed use reveal itself before the effect commits. Protection therefore follows from what the task permits rather than from how an attack is built, and applies uniformly across capability units without attack-specific policies or taint tracking. Against 13 baselines, APEX attains 0\% attack success on five of six benchmarks and 0.56\% on the sixth, holds 0\% under adaptive attacks on all three capability-unit types, and remains effective across defender backbones. Code is available at [URL].
tldr: APEX is an active-defense framework that protects LLM agents from indirect prompt injection by enforcing authorization and information-endorsement checks at the execution boundary where internal state becomes external action.
motivation: Indirect prompt injection hides adversarial instructions in runtime content read by LLM agents, and as agents compose more capability units (tools, MCP servers, skills) the attack carriers multiply, outpacing pattern-based defenses.
method: APEX shifts from attack-pattern coverage to a single stable enforcement point: a pre-compiled authorization contract derived from the trusted task admits an effect only if the contract justifies it, while runtime information is required to be endorsed by that task before the effect commits.
